subject: ss
title: Economics: Scarcity, Markets, Money, and Policy
objectives: You will explain scarcity, identify the factors of production, and find the opportunity cost of a choice.
You will use supply and demand tables and graphs to find the equilibrium price, a shortage, or a surplus, and predict how events and price controls affect a market.
You will compare market, command, and mixed economies and explain how competition, monopoly, and antitrust law affect prices.
You will explain the three jobs of money, how banks earn money, and the roles of the FDIC and the Federal Reserve.
You will interpret GDP and inflation data and tell fiscal policy from monetary policy using neutral, evidence-based language.

slides.title: Economics: Scarcity, Markets, Money, and Policy
slides.board:
Week 7 Social Studies: Economics

Today you will:

  • Explain scarcity and find the opportunity cost of a choice
  • Read supply and demand tables and graphs; predict shifts
  • Compare economic systems; explain competition and monopoly
  • Explain money, banks, the FDIC, and the Federal Reserve
  • Read GDP and inflation data; tell fiscal from monetary policy

Plan: Warm-up → six big ideas → we do it together → you do it → GED questions

notes.say: Economics is about 15 percent of the GED Social Studies test, and it is the part of social studies you already live every day: paying bills, comparing prices, deciding whether to pick up an extra shift. Almost every GED economics question hands you a table, a graph, or a short reading first, so today we learn the ideas and the reading moves together. By the end, a supply and demand table or an inflation chart should feel like something you can take apart in under two minutes.
ask: Think of one price you have noticed going up or down this year. What do you think caused it? (Expected: any honest answer, such as gas, eggs, or rent. Keep it on the board; we will explain it with supply and demand later today.)
notes.watch: Money topics can feel personal. Keep examples practical and respectful, and remind the student that GED economics questions ask what the data and readings show, not what anyone should think about a policy.

slides.title: Warm-up: Week 6 Review
slides.board:
Answer each one.

  1. Put in order: Pearl Harbor; end of Reconstruction; Civil Rights Act; stock market crash.
  2. About what share of American workers were unemployed in 1933?
  3. The FDIC (1933) was part of which New Deal "R": relief, recovery, or reform?
  4. What was the U.S. Cold War policy of stopping the spread of communism called?
steps: 1. End of Reconstruction (1877) → stock market crash (1929) → Pearl Harbor (1941) → Civil Rights Act (1964).
2. About one in four (about 25 percent).
3. Reform. Insuring bank deposits was meant to prevent another wave of bank failures.
4. Containment.

notes.say: These four questions review last week, and two of them lead straight into today. The Great Depression is the most famous economic crisis in American history: about a quarter of workers had no job, and thousands of banks failed. The FDIC was the reform Congress created so that families would not lose their savings again, and we will meet it later today. Give the student about three minutes, have them say each answer, then reveal.
ask: Why would insuring bank deposits help stop bank failures? (Expected: people would not rush to pull their money out if they knew it was safe)
notes.answer: 1. Reconstruction ends (1877), crash (1929), Pearl Harbor (1941), Civil Rights Act (1964). 2. About 25 percent. 3. Reform. 4. Containment.
notes.watch: If the student puts Pearl Harbor before the crash, anchor the dates: crash 1929, Roosevelt 1933, Pearl Harbor 1941. The Depression came first, and the war ended it.

slides.title: Scarcity Forces Choices
slides.board:
Scarcity: wants are unlimited, but resources (money, time, materials, workers) are limited.
Trade-off: choosing one thing means giving up another.
Opportunity cost: the value of the next best alternative you give up. One option, not the total of all of them.

Factor of productionMeaningBakery example
LandNatural resourcesWheat, water
LaborHuman workBakers, cashier
CapitalTools, machines, buildingsOvens, mixers
EntrepreneurshipRisk-taking that combines the othersThe owner who opened it

notes.say: Economics is the study of how people, businesses, and governments make choices about limited resources. Because of scarcity, every choice has a trade-off, and economists put a name on what you give up: the opportunity cost. Stress the words next best. If you had three options and picked one, the opportunity cost is only the one you would have picked instead, because you could never have done all of them. The factors of production are the resources used to make anything. Watch the word capital: in economics it means tools and machines, not money in the bank.
ask: A city spends $2 million on a new fire truck instead of a park. What is the trade-off? (Expected: the park it could have built with that money)
A delivery van is which factor of production? (Expected: capital)
notes.watch: Students often call money "capital." On the GED, capital means tools, machines, and buildings used to produce goods and services.

slides.title: Worked Example: What Did Jordan Give Up?
slides.board:
Jordan has a free Saturday. He can work an extra shift for $120, help a friend move for $60, or go to a free GED workshop. He goes to the workshop. He says that if he had skipped it, he would have worked the shift.

What is the opportunity cost of the workshop?
steps: Step 1: What did he choose? The workshop.
Step 2: What was his next best choice? He tells us: the $120 shift.
Step 3: Name it. The opportunity cost is the $120 shift.
Rule out the traps: Not $180 ($120 + $60), because he could only use the Saturday once. Not "nothing" just because the workshop was free: he still gave up $120.

notes.say: Walk through the three steps aloud, and then name both traps, because those are exactly the wrong answers the GED offers. The "free" trap is especially common: something can cost zero dollars and still have an opportunity cost, because your time is scarce too.
ask: If Jordan had said he would have helped his friend instead, what would the opportunity cost be? (Expected: helping the friend move, worth $60)
notes.watch: If the student says $180, ask: "Could Jordan have done both the shift and the move on the same Saturday?"

slides.title: We Do: Costs and Resources
slides.board:
1. A family has $300 left this month. They can fix the car, buy school clothes, or take a weekend trip. They fix the car; school clothes were their second choice. Opportunity cost?
  2. Classify each for a pizza shop: (a) the pizza oven, (b) tomatoes, (c) the delivery driver, (d) the owner who borrowed money to open it.
  3. Why does a government face scarcity too?
steps: 1. The school clothes, their next best choice. The trip is not included.
2. (a) Capital (b) Land (natural resource) (c) Labor (d) Entrepreneurship
3. Its tax money is limited too. A dollar spent on one program cannot also be spent on another or returned as a tax cut.

notes.say: Do these together. For number 1, have the student say the "next best" rule before answering. For number 2, ask which column of our table each one fits. Number 3 matters for later today: when Congress decides on taxes and spending, it is making trade-offs with scarce resources, just like a family.
ask: For 2(b), why are tomatoes "land"? (Expected: they come from natural resources: soil, water, and sun)
notes.answer: 1. School clothes. 2. (a) capital, (b) land, (c) labor, (d) entrepreneurship. 3. Government revenue is limited, so every spending choice gives up another use.
notes.watch: Students may call tomatoes "capital" because the shop bought them. Capital is a tool that is used again and again to make the product; ingredients are natural resources used up in production.

slides.title: Supply, Demand, and Equilibrium
slides.board:
• Law of demand: price up → quantity demanded down
  • Law of supply: price up → quantity supplied up
  • Equilibrium: demanded = supplied (where the lines cross)
  • Shortage: demanded > supplied (price too low)
  • Surplus: supplied > demanded (price too high)
  • Size: larger quantity − smaller quantity

figure.title: Movie Tickets per Week at a Small Theater

notes.say: Demand is how much buyers are willing and able to buy at each price; supply is how much sellers are willing and able to offer. Buyers and sellers react to price in opposite directions, which is why the two lines cross. Where they cross, the amount people want equals the amount offered: that is the equilibrium price, and markets tend to move toward it. If the price is set too low, buyers are left short: a shortage. If it is set too high, extra sits unsold: a surplus. On this graph the price is on the horizontal axis. Economists usually put price on the vertical axis, so always read the labels first.
ask: On the graph, at what price do the lines cross? (Expected: $10)
At $14, which is bigger, quantity demanded or quantity supplied? (Expected: quantity supplied, 300 compared with 100)
notes.watch: Students mix up shortage and surplus. Use the word itself: a shortage means buyers come up short. A surplus means extra is left over on the shelf.

slides.title: Worked Example: Reading the Ticket Table
slides.board:
Price$6$8$10$12$14
Demanded300250200150100
Supplied100150200250300

(a) Equilibrium price? (b) What happens at $14? (c) At $8?
steps: (a) Find the column where the numbers match: at $10, 200 = 200. Equilibrium price = $10, quantity = 200 tickets.
(b) At $14: supplied 300, demanded 100. Supplied is bigger, so a surplus.
Size: 300 − 100 = 200 extra tickets.
(c) At $8: demanded 250, supplied 150. Demanded is bigger, so a shortage of 250 − 150 = 100 tickets.

notes.say: Model the routine every time: find the price, read both numbers, decide which is bigger, name it, then subtract. Say the label of each row out loud so the student never reads the wrong row. Point out that prices above $10 all give surpluses and prices below $10 all give shortages.
ask: What happens at $12? (Expected: a surplus of 250 − 150 = 100 tickets)
notes.watch: If the student says "a shortage of 200" at $14, they read the size right but the direction wrong. Ask: "Are buyers left without tickets, or are tickets left without buyers?"

slides.title: What Shifts Demand or Supply?
slides.board:
Demand shifters (buyers)

  • Income
  • Tastes and trends
  • Price of a substitute (tea for coffee)
  • Price of a complement (printers and ink)
  • Expectations about the future

Supply shifters (sellers)

  • Cost of materials or labor
  • Technology
  • Weather and disasters
  • Taxes on producers
  • Number of sellers

Demand up or supply down → price up. Demand down or supply up → price down.

Price ceiling (legal maximum) below equilibrium → shortage. Price floor (legal minimum) above equilibrium → surplus.

notes.say: A change in a product's own price just moves along the curve. Everything else on this board shifts the whole curve. The key question is always: does this event change what buyers want, or what sellers can offer? Substitutes are goods used instead of each other; complements are goods used together. Governments sometimes set price controls. A price ceiling is a legal maximum, such as rent control; a price floor is a legal minimum, such as a minimum wage. Supporters point to fairness and affordability, and critics point to shortages or surpluses. The GED asks what the data show, not which side is right.
ask: Coffee prices rise. What happens to demand for tea? (Expected: it increases, because tea is a substitute)
A city sets the maximum rent at $900 when the equilibrium rent is $1,200. What results? (Expected: a shortage of apartments)
notes.watch: Students put weather events under demand ("people stop buying"). Ask: "Did buyers change their minds, or can farmers grow less?"

slides.title: Worked Example: A Freeze Hits the Orange Groves
slides.board:
A hard freeze destroys much of the orange crop in a major growing region.

What happens to the supply of oranges, the price, and the quantity sold?
steps: Step 1: Buyers or sellers? The freeze hits growers, so this is a supply event.
Step 2: Which direction? Fewer oranges can be produced, so supply decreases.
Step 3: Result. With fewer oranges at every price, the price rises and the quantity sold falls.
Rule out the trap: Demand did not decrease. Buyers still want oranges; there are simply fewer to sell.

notes.say: Teach the three-step routine and have the student say it back: buyers or sellers, which direction, what happens to price. Every shift question on the GED can be answered this way. Then connect it to the student's price from the title slide.
ask: What happens to the price of orange juice, which is made from oranges? (Expected: it likely rises too, because an input became more expensive, which decreases the supply of juice)
notes.watch: If the student says "people buy fewer oranges, so demand falls," separate the cause from the result: the quantity bought falls because supply fell and the price rose.

slides.title: We Do: Buyers or Sellers?
slides.board:
For each event, name the shift and what happens to the price.

  1. A widely shared study says blueberries improve memory.
  2. Gas prices jump sharply. What happens in the market for large SUVs?
  3. New robots cut the cost of making phones.
  4. A city sets a maximum rent of $900. The equilibrium rent is $1,100.
steps: 1. Tastes change (buyers): demand increases, price rises.
2. Gas and SUVs are used together (complements): demand for SUVs decreases, price falls.
3. Technology lowers costs (sellers): supply increases, price falls.
4. A price ceiling below equilibrium: more renters want apartments than landlords offer, so a shortage.

notes.say: Have the student answer "buyers or sellers" first for each one, then the direction, then the price. Number 2 is the hardest: the price of gas is not the price of SUVs, so it shifts SUV demand. Number 4 connects back to the table: a price held below equilibrium always lands on a shortage row.
ask: In number 2, what kind of goods are gas and SUVs? (Expected: complements, used together)
notes.answer: 1. Demand up, price up. 2. Demand for SUVs down, price down. 3. Supply up, price down. 4. Shortage.
notes.watch: On number 3, some students say "demand increases because phones are cheaper." The cheaper price is the result of the supply shift, not a demand shift.

slides.title: Economic Systems and Competition
slides.board:
SystemWho decides what is made and the price?
MarketBuyers and sellers (Adam Smith's "invisible hand," 1776)
CommandThe government
Mixed (United States)Mostly markets, plus government rules and services
  • Competition (many sellers) → lower prices, better quality
  • Oligopoly: a few large sellers (airlines)
  • Monopoly: one seller, no close substitutes → can charge more
  • Sherman Antitrust Act (1890): bans price fixing and unfair tactics to build or keep a monopoly

notes.say: Every economy must answer what to produce, how to produce it, and who gets it. In a market economy, prices and private choices answer those questions. In a command economy, the government does. The United States has a mixed economy: mostly markets, with government rules on safety and fair competition, and public services like roads and schools. Competition is the engine of a market: when buyers can switch, sellers must offer better prices and quality. A monopoly removes that pressure. Being the only seller is not illegal by itself, but the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 bans agreeing with competitors to fix prices and using unfair tactics to create or keep a monopoly.
ask: Why does competition tend to lower prices? (Expected: buyers can switch to another seller, so each seller must offer a better deal)
Is it illegal to be the only seller in a market? (Expected: not by itself; price fixing and unfair tactics are illegal)
notes.watch: Students often say every monopoly is illegal. Correct it with the Sherman Act's actual targets: price fixing and unfair tactics.

slides.title: Worked Example: A New Airline on the Route
slides.board:
For years, only Coastal Air flew between Dunmore and Port Ellis. A round trip cost $480. In March, a low-cost airline began flying the same route for $220. By September, Coastal's round-trip fare was $260.

What best explains Coastal's price change, and what does the passage NOT show?
steps: Step 1: Before. One seller on the route: a monopoly on that route, with a $480 fare.
Step 2: What changed? A competitor entered with a much lower fare.
Step 3: Result. Coastal cut its fare by $480 − $260 = $220. Competition pushed the price down, because travelers could switch.
Not shown: that Coastal broke the law (being the only seller was not illegal) or what will happen next year.

notes.say: This is the classic GED competition story: one seller, a new rival, a lower price. Model how to state the conclusion the passage supports, and then name two tempting claims it does not support. That second move is what earns points on "best supported" questions.
ask: What would the antitrust laws forbid Coastal and the new airline from doing? (Expected: secretly agreeing to charge the same high fare)
notes.watch: Students sometimes write "Coastal lost money." The passage does not say that. Keep them inside the text.

slides.title: Money, Banks, the FDIC, and the Fed
slides.board:
Three jobs of money: medium of exchange (you buy with it) · unit of account (prices are measured in it) · store of value (you can save it)

  • Banks take deposits, lend much of the money out, pay savers interest, and charge borrowers a higher rate. The difference is a main source of profit.
  • FDIC (1933): insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category.
  • Federal Reserve (1913): the central bank. A bank for banks and the federal government, not for individuals. Supervises banks and runs monetary policy; goals of maximum employment and stable prices.

notes.say: Before money, people bartered: you had to find someone who had what you wanted and wanted what you had. Money solves that by doing three jobs. A bank is a business: it might pay 1 percent on savings and charge 7 percent on a car loan, and that gap pays its bills. Because banks lend out most deposits, a rush of withdrawals can sink a bank, which is what happened thousands of times in the early Depression. Congress answered with the FDIC in 1933. The Federal Reserve is older, created by Congress in 1913. You cannot open an account there; it serves banks and the government.
ask: A price tag says $4.99. Which job of money is that? (Expected: unit of account)
Which agency would pay you back if your insured bank failed? (Expected: the FDIC)
notes.watch: The FDIC and the Fed get swapped constantly. Anchor them: FDIC = insurance on deposits (1933); Fed = central bank and interest rates (1913).

slides.title: Worked Example: How a Bank Earns and What Is Insured
slides.board:
Riverside Bank holds $10 million in savings deposits and pays savers 1% interest a year. It lends $8 million in car loans at 6%.

(a) How much does the bank earn from the gap in a year (before other costs)?

(b) Maria has $280,000 in one individual savings account there. The bank fails. How much is insured?
steps: Interest paid to savers: $10,000,000 × 0.01 = $100,000.
Interest earned on loans: $8,000,000 × 0.06 = $480,000.
(a) $480,000 − $100,000 = $380,000 from the interest gap.
(b) The limit is $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category. Maria has one individual account, so $250,000 is insured and $280,000 − $250,000 = $30,000 is not.

notes.say: The math is simple, but it shows the business model of every bank: borrow from savers cheaply, lend to borrowers at a higher rate. For part (b), read the FDIC rule slowly. The limit is per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, so one person with one individual account at one bank is covered up to $250,000.
ask: How could Maria have had all of her money insured? (Expected: for example, by keeping some of it at a second insured bank)
notes.watch: Some students answer that $280,000 is insured "because it is in a bank." Insurance has a limit; anything above it is not covered.

slides.title: We Do: Money and Banking
slides.board:
Name the job of money in 1–3. Then answer 4 and 5.

  1. A menu lists a burger at $9.
  2. You hand the cashier $20 for groceries.
  3. You keep $500 in savings for next year's car registration.
  4. Which agency sets the nation's monetary policy?
  5. True or false: you can open a checking account at the Federal Reserve.
steps: 1. Unit of account: the price measures value.
2. Medium of exchange: money is traded for goods.
3. Store of value: money holds value until later.
4. The Federal Reserve. 5. False. The Fed serves banks and the federal government, not individuals.

notes.say: Have the student name the job before you reveal each one, and ask for the clue: a price is measuring, a payment is exchanging, savings is storing. Then check the two agencies again, since they are the most confused pair in this lesson.
ask: Why does high inflation make money a weaker store of value? (Expected: saved money buys less later)
notes.answer: 1. Unit of account. 2. Medium of exchange. 3. Store of value. 4. The Federal Reserve. 5. False.
notes.watch: Numbers 1 and 2 both have a dollar amount. Ask: "Is money changing hands, or is it just measuring a price?"

slides.title: Measuring the Economy: GDP and Inflation
slides.board:
• GDP: total market value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a period
  • Real GDP: adjusted for inflation, so it shows whether output truly grew
  • Recession: real GDP falls and unemployment rises for a sustained time
  • Inflation: a general rise in prices; each dollar buys less

Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100

figure.title: Real GDP of Country Q (billions of dollars)

notes.say: GDP is the most common measure of the size of an economy. It counts only final goods, so the flour sold to a bakery is not counted separately from the bread. Real GDP strips out price increases: if prices rose 5 percent and GDP rose 5 percent, the country did not actually produce more. When real GDP falls and many people lose jobs, that is a recession. Two quarters of falling GDP in a row is a common rule of thumb, though official U.S. recession dates are set by economists at the National Bureau of Economic Research. Inflation is usually measured by the Consumer Price Index from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and the Federal Reserve aims for about 2 percent a year over time.
ask: On the graph, between which years did real GDP fall? (Expected: Year 3 to Year 4, from 546 to 530)
By what percent did real GDP grow from Year 1 to Year 2? (Expected: 20 ÷ 500 = 4%)
notes.watch: Students divide by the new value. Percent change always divides by the starting (old) value.

slides.title: Worked Example: Inflation and Your Paycheck
slides.board:
A basket of household goods cost $80 last year and $84 this year. Terrell's hourly pay rose from $18.00 to $18.54.

(a) What was the inflation rate? (b) Did Terrell's purchasing power rise or fall?
steps: Prices: $84 − $80 = $4. Then 4 ÷ 80 = 0.05 = 5% inflation.
Pay: $18.54 − $18.00 = $0.54. Then 0.54 ÷ 18.00 = 0.03 = 3% raise.
Compare: prices rose 5%, pay rose 3%. Prices grew faster.
(b) Purchasing power fell. Terrell earns more dollars, but each hour of work buys less.

notes.say: This is one of the most common GED economics tasks: compare two percent changes. Model each calculation line by line. Then hammer the idea: a raise in dollars is not a raise in what you can buy if prices rise faster. Economists call the pay adjusted for prices "real wages."
ask: If Terrell's pay had risen 6% instead, what would have happened to his purchasing power? (Expected: it would have risen, because 6% is more than 5%)
notes.watch: If the student gets 4.8% for inflation, they divided 4 by 84, the new price. Divide by the starting price, $80.

slides.title: Fiscal Policy vs. Monetary Policy
slides.board:
Fiscal policyMonetary policy
Who decidesCongress and the PresidentThe Federal Reserve
ToolsTaxes and government spendingInterest rates and the money supply
To boost a weak economyCut taxes or spend moreLower interest rates
To cool high inflationRaise taxes or spend lessRaise interest rates

Memory hook: Fiscal = federal budget. Monetary = money and rates.

notes.say: Ask two questions about any policy: who acted, and what tool did they use? Fiscal policy is taxing and spending, passed by Congress and signed by the President; the Constitution even says revenue bills must start in the House of Representatives. Monetary policy belongs to the Federal Reserve. When the Fed raises its target interest rate, loans for cars, homes, and businesses get more expensive, so people borrow and spend less and price pressure eases. Lower rates do the opposite. Economists and leaders disagree about which tools to use and when; on the GED, your job is to identify each side and its evidence.
ask: Congress votes to cut income taxes. Fiscal or monetary? (Expected: fiscal)
Why would higher interest rates slow inflation? (Expected: borrowing costs more, so people and businesses spend less)
notes.watch: Students think the President or Congress sets interest rates. The Federal Reserve sets its target rate; Congress created the Fed but does not vote on rates.

slides.title: Worked Example: Who Acted, With What Tool?
slides.board:
Classify each action, and say what it is meant to do.

  1. Congress passes a law that lowers income tax rates for two years.
  2. The Federal Reserve raises its target interest rate.
  3. Congress approves $40 billion to repair bridges and roads.
steps: 1. Who: Congress. Tool: taxes. Fiscal policy, meant to leave people more money to spend and boost the economy.
2. Who: the Fed. Tool: interest rates. Monetary policy, meant to slow borrowing and cool inflation.
3. Who: Congress. Tool: spending. Fiscal policy, meant to put money into the economy and create jobs (as well as fix roads).
Pattern: anything Congress votes on is fiscal; anything about the Fed and rates is monetary.

notes.say: Model the two questions for every action, out loud, before naming the policy. Then add the purpose, because GED drop-down items often ask both the label and the goal.
ask: Which of these three would a critic most likely say adds to the national debt? (Expected: 1 or 3, since tax cuts and new spending can increase borrowing if revenue falls short)
notes.watch: If the student says number 2 is fiscal because "the government did it," point out that the Fed is not Congress. The tool, interest rates, tells you it is monetary.

slides.title: We Do: Data and Policy
slides.board:
1. Real GDP rose from $500 billion to $520 billion. Growth rate?
  2. A price index rose from 150 to 159. Inflation rate?
  3. During a recession, the Fed lowers rates. Fiscal or monetary? Goal?
  4. "The new highway bill is the smartest law Congress has passed in decades." Fact or opinion?
steps: 2. 159 − 150 = 9; 9 ÷ 150 = 0.06 = 6%.
3. Monetary; cheaper borrowing is meant to encourage spending and help the economy recover.
4. Opinion: "smartest" is a judgment people can disagree with.

notes.say: Have the student talk through each percent change: subtract, divide by the old value, convert. Number 4 is a reminder that economics questions on the GED also test fact versus opinion, especially about policies. Judgment words like best, smartest, worst, and should signal an opinion.
ask: In number 2, what would you get if you divided by the new value? (Expected: 9 ÷ 159 ≈ 5.7%, which is wrong)
notes.answer: 1. 4%. 2. 6%. 3. Monetary; to boost spending in a weak economy. 4. Opinion.

slides.title: You Do 1: Scarcity and Supply and Demand
slides.board:
On your own (4 minutes).

  1. Tasha can work a $75 shift, go to a cookout, or study. She studies; otherwise she would have worked. Opportunity cost?
  2. A bakery's delivery van is which factor of production?
  3. At $4, buyers want 500 cups of coffee and sellers offer 350. Shortage or surplus? How big?
  4. A new factory starts making e-bikes. What happens to the supply and price of e-bikes?
steps: 1. The $75 shift. 2. Capital. 3. Shortage of 500 − 350 = 150 cups. 4. Supply increases; the price tends to fall.

notes.say: Start a four-minute timer and stay quiet. When time is up, have the student give all four answers before you reveal, and ask for the reason behind number 3 (which number was bigger) and number 4 (buyers or sellers).
notes.answer: 1. The $75 shift. 2. Capital. 3. Shortage of 150 cups. 4. Supply up, price down.
notes.watch: On number 3, "surplus of 150" means the student mixed up the direction: demanded is bigger, so buyers are left short.

slides.title: You Do 2: Markets, Money, and Banks
slides.board:
On your own (4 minutes).

  1. The government decides what factories make and sets all prices. What kind of economy?
  2. One company is the only electricity seller in a town, with no close substitutes. What is this market called?
  3. A price tag reads $3.99. Which job of money?
  4. Ben has $310,000 in one individual account at one insured bank. How much is not covered by the FDIC?
steps: 1. Command economy. 2. Monopoly. 3. Unit of account. 4. $310,000 − $250,000 = $60,000.

notes.say: Same routine: four minutes, quiet, then the student reports. For number 4, have them say the FDIC limit and the subtraction out loud.
notes.watch: If the student answers $250,000 for number 4, they found the insured amount. The question asks what is not covered.

slides.title: You Do 3: GDP, Inflation, and Policy
slides.board:
On your own (4 minutes).

  1. A price index rose from 200 to 206. Inflation rate?
  2. Real GDP went from $900 billion to $873 billion. Percent change?
  3. Congress increases spending on schools. Fiscal or monetary?
  4. To cool high inflation, does the Federal Reserve usually raise or lower interest rates?
steps: 1. 6 ÷ 200 = 0.03 = 3%. 2. −27 ÷ 900 = −0.03, a 3% decrease. 3. Fiscal. 4. Raise.

notes.say: Four minutes. For numbers 1 and 2, the student must say the subtraction, the division by the old value, and the conversion to a percent. For number 2, make sure they say "decrease," not just "3 percent."
notes.watch: A student who answers 2.9% on number 1 divided by 206. Divide by the starting value.

slides.title: GED Question 1: A Price Ceiling
slides.board:
Weekly parking passes at a downtown garage:

Price$40$50$60$70$80
Demanded500420340260180
Supplied180260340420500

The city sets a maximum price of $50 per pass. What will most likely result?

A. A surplus of 160 passes
B. A shortage of 160 passes
C. A shortage of 80 passes
D. No change, because $50 is the equilibrium price
steps: Eliminate D. Equilibrium is where the rows match: $60 (340 = 340), not $50.
Eliminate A. At $50, demanded (420) is bigger than supplied (260). That is a shortage, not a surplus.
Eliminate C. 80 comes from 340 − 260, comparing with the equilibrium quantity. Compare the two quantities at $50.
Answer B. A maximum below equilibrium is a price ceiling: 420 − 260 = 160 passes short.

notes.say: Have the student commit to an answer before you reveal anything, then walk the eliminations. Each wrong option is a real mistake: misreading the equilibrium, flipping the direction, or subtracting the wrong numbers. Naming those mistakes is how the student learns to spot them on test day.
ask: If the city instead set a minimum price of $70, what would happen? (Expected: a surplus of 420 − 260 = 160 passes)
notes.answer: B. A shortage of 160 passes (420 demanded − 260 supplied at $50).
notes.watch: Students see "maximum" and think "too much," choosing surplus. A maximum price holds the price down, which leaves buyers short.

slides.title: GED Question 2: Wages and Prices
slides.board:

Which conclusion is best supported by the data?

A. Rising wages caused the inflation in Year 2.
B. Workers' purchasing power fell in Years 2 and 3.
C. Workers' purchasing power fell in every year shown.

steps: Eliminate A. The table shows two numbers side by side, not what caused either one. "Caused" goes beyond the data.
Eliminate C. In Year 1 (3% > 2%) and Year 4 (5% > 3%), wages grew faster than prices, so purchasing power rose.
Eliminate D. This is a prediction. The data stop at Year 4.
Answer B. In Year 2 (4% < 6%) and Year 3 (4% < 5%), prices rose faster than wages, so purchasing power fell.

notes.say: Teach the comparison routine: for each year, which is bigger, wage growth or inflation? Write a plus or minus above each column. Then use the same three trap types from Week 1: causes the data cannot prove, claims that go too far ("every"), and predictions.
ask: In which year did purchasing power rise the most? (Expected: Year 4, where wages beat inflation by 2 points)
notes.answer: B. Wage growth was below inflation in Years 2 and 3, so purchasing power fell in those years.
notes.watch: A is the trap: it sounds like real economics. Ask: "Where does the table say what caused anything?"

slides.title: GED Strategy: Three Questions for Economics Items
slides.board:
1. Labels first. Title, axis or column labels, units (dollars, billions, percent). Which row is demanded and which is supplied?
  2. Buyers or sellers? For any event, decide who it affects before you decide the direction.
  3. Who acted, with what tool? Congress + taxes/spending = fiscal. The Fed + interest rates = monetary.

Math: do percent change on scratch paper: (new − old) ÷ old.

Policy: answer what each side says, not who is right.

notes.say: Most wrong answers on economics items come from three slips: reading the right number in the wrong row, putting a supply event under demand, and mixing up who runs fiscal and monetary policy. These three questions catch all of them. Have the student say the three questions back to you. At about two minutes per question, the ten seconds spent on labels is the best time investment on the test.
ask: Which of the three questions would you use for "A drought hits wheat farms"? (Expected: buyers or sellers: sellers, so supply)
notes.watch: Strong students rush past the labels. On the next practice item, make them read the labels aloud before they look at a single number.

screens.title: What You Will Learn
screens.html:
Economics is about 15 percent of the GED Social Studies test, and it is the subject you use every day: paying bills, comparing prices, deciding whether to take an extra shift, or wondering why groceries cost more this year. Most GED economics questions give you a table, a graph, or a short reading first.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Explain scarcity and find the opportunity cost of a choice
  • Use supply and demand tables and graphs to find the equilibrium price, a shortage, or a surplus, and predict how events shift supply or demand
  • Compare economic systems and explain how competition and monopoly affect prices
  • Explain the jobs of money, how banks earn money, and the roles of the FDIC and the Federal Reserve
  • Read GDP and inflation data and tell fiscal policy from monetary policy

Each screen teaches one idea and ends with a quick check. Answer it before you move on.

screens.title: Scarcity and Trade-offs
screens.html:
Economics is the study of how people, businesses, and governments make choices about using limited resources.

Scarcity means that wants are unlimited, but the resources to meet them (money, time, materials, workers) are limited.

Because of scarcity, every choice has a trade-off: choosing one thing means giving up something else. A family with $500 left for the month cannot buy everything on its list. A worker with one free evening cannot both work overtime and go to a class. A city with $2 million cannot both build a park and buy a fire truck that costs $2 million.

Scarcity is not the same as being poor. Even a very rich person or country has only 24 hours in a day and a limited amount of land, workers, and materials. Everyone faces trade-offs.

check.prompt: Which statement best explains why every choice has a trade-off?
options: Resources such as time and money are limited, so using them one way means giving up another use.
Prices go up whenever many people want the same product at the same time.
The government decides how most money and time in the country will be used.
People want only the things they can afford, so they never run short.
why: That describes the law of demand and prices, not the reason choices have trade-offs. Trade-offs exist because resources are limited.
That describes a command economy. Even where people make their own choices, they face trade-offs because resources are limited.
This reverses scarcity. Wants are unlimited; it is resources that run short.
check.hint: What is limited, and what is unlimited?
check.explain: A trade-off happens because resources are scarce: time, money, and materials are limited, so using them for one thing means you cannot use them for another. The statement about prices describes demand, not trade-offs, and wants are unlimited, not limited to what people can afford.

screens.title: Opportunity Cost
screens.html:
Opportunity cost = the value of the next best alternative you give up when you make a choice.

Two rules keep you out of trouble:

  • Only the next best option counts. If you had three choices and picked one, the opportunity cost is the one you would have picked instead, not the total of the other two. You could never have done all of them.
  • "Free" still has a cost. A free class still costs the time you could have spent doing something else, such as working a paid shift.

On the GED, the question usually tells you which option was the next best. Look for words like "would have," "second choice," or "otherwise."

example.prompt: Keisha has a free evening. She could work overtime for $90, watch a movie with friends, or study for the GED. She studies. She says she would have worked overtime if she had not studied. What is her opportunity cost?
steps: What did she choose? Studying.
What was her next best choice? Overtime, worth $90.
Rule out the rest: the movie is not part of the cost; she could not have done all three.
example.answer: The opportunity cost is the $90 she could have earned working overtime.

check.prompt:
Rosa can spend Sunday cleaning houses for $85, selling crafts at a fair for about $60, or resting at home. She chooses to clean houses. She says that if she had not, she would have sold crafts at the fair. What is the dollar value of her opportunity cost?

$

mistakes.why: $85 is what Rosa chose (cleaning houses). The opportunity cost is what she gave up: her next best choice.
You added two options together, but Rosa could only spend Sunday one way. Count only her next best choice, the craft fair.

check.hint: Which option does Rosa say she would have picked instead?
check.explain: Rosa chose cleaning houses. Her next best choice, in her own words, was selling crafts, worth about $60. That is her opportunity cost. The $85 is what she gained, not what she gave up, and resting was her third choice.

screens.title: The Factors of Production
screens.html:
Businesses use four kinds of resources, called the factors of production, to make goods and services.

FactorMeaningExample: a bakery
LandNatural resourcesWheat, water, sugar
LaborHuman work and skillBakers, cashier
CapitalTools, machines, buildings used to produceOvens, mixers, delivery van
EntrepreneurshipThe risk-taking that combines the other threeThe owner who invested savings to open it

In economics, capital means tools and machines, not money in the bank. Ingredients that get used up are natural resources (land), not capital.

check.prompt: A furniture shop uses each resource below. Drag each one into the factor of production it represents.
choices: Oak timber cut from a forest
The hours a carpenter spends building chairs
The owner who risked her savings to open the shop
check.why: The most common mistake is calling the owner “labor.” The owner may also work, but taking the risk of starting and running the business is entrepreneurship.
check.hint: Is it a natural resource, human work, a tool, or the risk of starting the business?
check.explain:
• Oak timber: a natural resource, so land.
  • Carpenter's hours: human work, so labor.
  • Power saw and delivery truck: tools and machines used again and again, so capital.
  • Owner who risked her savings: entrepreneurship.

screens.title: The Laws of Demand and Supply
screens.html:
Demand is how much of a product buyers are willing and able to buy at each price. Supply is how much sellers are willing and able to offer at each price.

Law of demand
Price goes up → buyers buy less.
Price goes down → buyers buy more.

Law of supply
Price goes up → sellers offer more.
Price goes down → sellers offer less.

Why? A higher price makes buyers look for substitutes or go without, while it makes selling more profitable, so sellers want to produce more. Buyers and sellers react to price in opposite directions. That is why, on a graph, the demand line and the supply line slope opposite ways and cross.

check.prompt: A stadium raises the price of a soda from $4 to $6, and nothing else changes. According to the law of demand, what will most likely happen?
options: Fans will buy fewer sodas than they did at $4.
Fans will buy more sodas, since a higher price signals better quality.
The stadium will want to sell fewer sodas than it did at $4.
Fans will buy the same number, since they cannot bring drinks into the game.
why: This reverses the law of demand. When the price rises and nothing else changes, buyers buy less, not more.
This mixes up the law of supply. A higher price makes sellers want to sell more, not fewer, and the question asks about buyers.
The law of demand says quantity demanded falls when price rises. Some fans will skip a drink or buy one instead of two, even at a stadium.
check.hint: Does a higher price make buyers want more or less?
check.explain: The law of demand says that as price rises, quantity demanded falls. At $6, some fans will skip a soda or buy fewer. A higher price makes the seller want to offer more (the law of supply), but the question asks about buyers.

screens.title: Equilibrium, Shortage, and Surplus
screens.html:
The equilibrium price is the price where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied. On a graph, it is where the two lines cross. Markets tend to move toward this price.

Ticket price$6$8$10$12$14
Quantity demanded300250200150100
Quantity supplied100150200250300

Demanded = supplied → equilibrium
Demanded > supplied (price too low) → shortage
Supplied > demanded (price too high) → surplus
Size = larger number − smaller number

On this graph, price is on the horizontal axis. Many graphs put price on the vertical axis, so read the labels first.

figure.title: Movie Tickets per Week at a Small Theater

example.prompt: Use the table. What is the equilibrium price, and what happens if the theater charges $14?
steps: Find the matching column: at $10, 200 demanded and 200 supplied. Equilibrium = $10.
At $14, 300 are supplied but only 100 are demanded. Supplied is bigger, so there is a surplus.
example.answer: Equilibrium price $10; at $14, a surplus of 200 tickets.

check.prompt: Use the ticket table. If the theater charges $12, how many tickets per week will go unsold?

mistakes.why: That is the gap at $14 (300 − 100). Use the $12 column: 250 supplied − 150 demanded.
You added the two quantities. The size of a surplus is the difference: 250 − 150.

check.hint: Find the $12 column. Subtract the smaller quantity from the larger one.
check.explain: At $12, quantity supplied is 250 and quantity demanded is 150. Supplied is bigger, so there is a surplus: 250 − 150 = 100 tickets left unsold each week.

screens.title: What Shifts Demand?
screens.html:
A change in a product's own price does not shift demand; it just changes how much people buy. Other events that change what buyers want shift the whole demand curve:

  • Income: when incomes rise, people buy more of most goods, like restaurant meals.
  • Tastes and trends: a health study praising a food raises demand for it.
  • Price of a substitute (a good used instead): if tea gets expensive, more people buy coffee.
  • Price of a complement (a good used together): if printers get cheaper, people buy more printers and more ink.
  • Expectations: if people expect prices to rise next month, they buy more now.

Demand increases → price rises. Demand decreases → price falls.

check.prompt: The price of tea rises sharply. Tea and coffee are substitutes. What will most likely happen in the market for coffee?
options: Demand for coffee increases, as some tea drinkers switch to coffee.
Demand for coffee decreases, as people cut back on all hot drinks.
Supply of coffee decreases, as coffee growers switch over to tea.
Nothing changes, since only the price of tea itself has gone up.
why: That is how complements behave (goods used together). Tea and coffee are substitutes, so when tea costs more, people buy more coffee instead.
The event affects buyers' choices, not coffee growers' costs. Ask first: does this change what buyers want or what sellers can offer?
The price of tea is not the price of coffee. A change in a related good's price shifts the demand for coffee.
check.hint: Substitutes are used instead of each other. If one gets expensive, what do buyers do?
check.explain: Tea and coffee are substitutes. When tea gets more expensive, some tea drinkers switch to coffee, so demand for coffee increases (and its price tends to rise). A decrease in demand would fit complements, goods used together, not substitutes.

screens.title: What Shifts Supply?
screens.html:
Events that change what sellers can offer shift the supply curve:

  • Cost of inputs: if materials or wages cost more, sellers offer less.
  • Technology: better machines lower costs, so sellers offer more.
  • Weather and disasters: a drought or freeze cuts crop supplies.
  • Taxes on producers: a tax on each unit sold raises sellers' costs, so supply decreases.
  • Number of sellers: new businesses entering a market increase supply.

Supply decreases → price rises. Supply increases → price falls.

Three-step routine for any event: (1) Buyers or sellers? (2) Increase or decrease? (3) What happens to price?

example.prompt: A drought ruins much of the wheat harvest. What happens to the price of wheat?
steps: Buyers or sellers? Farmers, the sellers. This is a supply event.
Direction: less wheat can be grown, so supply decreases.
Price: when supply decreases, the price rises.
example.answer: Supply decreases, so the price of wheat rises and less wheat is sold.

check.prompt: The government places a new tax on paint manufacturers for every gallon they sell. What will most likely happen in the market for paint?
options: Supply decreases, and the price of paint rises.
Demand decreases, and the price of paint falls.
Supply increases, and the price of paint falls.
Supply decreases, and the price of paint falls.
why: The tax is placed on the companies that make paint, so it affects sellers, not buyers. That is a supply event.
A tax raises sellers' costs, so they offer less, not more. Higher costs decrease supply.
The direction of supply is right, but when supply decreases, there is less paint at every price, so the price rises.
check.hint: Who pays the tax, buyers or sellers? Does it make producing paint cheaper or more expensive?
check.explain: The tax falls on producers, so this is a supply event. It raises their cost for every gallon, so supply decreases. With less paint offered, the price rises. Calling this a demand change is the most common error: buyers did not change what they want.

screens.title: Price Ceilings and Price Floors
screens.html:
Sometimes the government sets a price by law instead of letting the market decide.

Price ceilingPrice floor
What it isA legal maximum priceA legal minimum price
ExampleRent controlMinimum wage
When it mattersSet below equilibriumSet above equilibrium
Likely resultShortage (buyers want more than is offered)Surplus (more is offered than buyers want)

Memory hook: a ceiling holds the price down, like a ceiling over your head; a floor holds it up.

People disagree about these policies. Supporters point to fairness and affordability; critics point to shortages or surpluses. GED questions ask what the data show, not which side is right.

check.prompt:
Complete the statements.

A law that sets the highest price sellers may charge is a {{0}}. If it is set below the equilibrium price, the most likely result is a {{1}}. A minimum wage set above the wage at which the number of workers seeking jobs equals the number of jobs offered is an example of a {{2}}.

options: price ceiling
price floor
tariff
subsidy
why: A price floor is a legal minimum, the lowest price allowed. This law sets the highest price.
A tariff is a tax on imported goods. It does not set a maximum price.
A subsidy is a government payment to producers or buyers. It does not set a maximum price.

options: shortage
surplus
equilibrium
why: A surplus happens when the price is held above equilibrium. Below equilibrium, buyers want more than sellers offer.
Equilibrium happens only at the market price. Holding the price below it means quantities no longer match.

options: price floor
price ceiling
monopoly
why: A minimum wage sets the lowest legal wage, so it is a floor, not a ceiling (a maximum).
A monopoly is a market with one seller. A minimum wage is a legal minimum price for labor.

check.hint: Ceiling = maximum (holds the price down). Floor = minimum (holds the price up).
check.explain: A legal maximum price is a price ceiling. Set below equilibrium, it makes buyers want more than sellers offer: a shortage. A minimum wage is a legal minimum price for labor, a price floor. Mixing up the two is the common error: remember that the ceiling is the top limit.

screens.title: Market, Command, and Mixed Economies
screens.html:
Every economy must answer three questions: What will be produced? How will it be produced? Who gets it?

SystemWho answers the questions?
Market economyBuyers and sellers, through prices and private choices
Command economyThe government decides what is made and sets prices
Mixed economyMostly markets, with government rules and public services

In The Wealth of Nations (1776), the Scottish writer Adam Smith described how people pursuing their own interests in a market are guided, "as if by an invisible hand," to serve others too. The United States has a mixed economy: private businesses make most goods, but the government sets safety rules, enforces fair competition, and provides services such as roads and public schools.

check.prompt: In the fictional country of Varden, private companies produce most goods and set their own prices. The government sets workplace safety rules, runs public schools, and enforces laws against price fixing. Which kind of economy does Varden have?
options: A mixed economy
A pure market economy
A command economy
An oligopoly
why: Private companies do set prices, but the government also makes rules and provides services. A pure market economy would leave those choices to buyers and sellers alone.
In a command economy the government decides what is made and sets prices. In Varden, private companies do that.
An oligopoly is a single market with a few large sellers, not a whole economic system.
check.hint: Who makes most decisions, and does the government also play a role?
check.explain: Private companies make most decisions, which is the market part, and the government sets rules and runs schools, which is the government part. That combination is a mixed economy, like the United States. It is not a command economy, because the government does not decide what is made or set prices.

screens.title: Competition and Monopoly
screens.html:
Competition among many sellers tends to push prices down and quality up, because buyers can switch to another seller.

  • Monopoly: a market with only one seller and no close substitutes. With no rivals, a monopoly can charge higher prices. Example: a town with only one water company.
  • Oligopoly: a market with a few large sellers, such as airlines or wireless phone service.

Congress passed the Sherman Antitrust Act in 1890, during the age of giant trusts you studied last week. It makes it illegal for companies to agree with competitors to fix prices or to use unfair tactics to create or keep a monopoly.

Being the only seller is not illegal by itself. A company that wins every customer with a better product breaks no law.

check.prompt: Which action would most clearly violate the Sherman Antitrust Act?
options: Two cement makers secretly agree to charge the same high price.
A bakery becomes the only one in town because customers like it best.
A grocery store cuts its prices to win customers from a rival store.
A small restaurant raises its prices after its food costs go up.
why: Being the only seller is not illegal by itself. Winning customers with a better product breaks no antitrust law.
Cutting prices to win customers is ordinary competition, which antitrust law is meant to protect.
Raising prices because costs went up is a normal business decision made alone, not an agreement with competitors.
check.hint: The act targets agreements between competitors and unfair tactics.
check.explain: The Sherman Antitrust Act makes it illegal for competitors to agree to fix prices. The two cement makers did exactly that. A bakery that becomes the only seller by being the best is a tempting wrong answer, but being the only seller is not illegal by itself.

screens.title: The Three Jobs of Money
screens.html:
Before money, people bartered: they traded goods directly. Barter is hard, because you must find someone who has what you want and wants what you have. Money solves that problem by doing three jobs.

JobMeaningExample
Medium of exchangeUsed to buy and sellPaying $20 for groceries
Unit of accountUsed to measure and compare valueA price tag of $4.99; comparing two phones
Store of valueHolds value over timeSaving $50 a week for a car repair

Quick test: Is money changing hands (exchange), measuring a price (account), or being saved for later (store)? Inflation weakens money as a store of value, because saved dollars buy less later.

check.prompt: Paying a mechanic $150 to fix your brakes uses money mainly as which of the following?
options: A medium of exchange
A unit of account
A store of value
A form of capital
why: Unit of account is money measuring value, like a price tag. Here money actually changes hands in a trade for a service.
Store of value is money saved for later. Here you are spending it now.
In economics, capital means tools and machines used in production, not one of the jobs of money.
check.hint: Is money changing hands, measuring a price, or being saved?
check.explain: You traded $150 for a service, so money worked as a medium of exchange. If you had only compared the mechanic's prices, that would be a unit of account; if you had saved the money for later, a store of value.

screens.title: How Banks Work and the FDIC
screens.html:
A bank is a business. It accepts deposits and pays savers interest, and it lends much of that money to borrowers, who pay a higher interest rate. A bank might pay 1 percent on savings and charge 7 percent on a car loan. The difference is a main source of the bank's profit.

Because banks lend out most deposits, a bank can fail if many loans go unpaid or too many depositors withdraw at once. Thousands of banks failed in the early years of the Great Depression, and families lost their savings. In response, Congress created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) in 1933.

The FDIC insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category. If an insured bank fails, depositors get their insured money back.

example.prompt: Maria has $280,000 in one individual savings account at an insured bank. The bank fails. How much of her money is insured?
steps: The limit is $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category.
Maria has one individual account at one bank, so the limit is $250,000.
$280,000 − $250,000 = $30,000 above the limit.

check.prompt:
Andre keeps $265,000 in one individual savings account at one FDIC-insured bank. He has no other accounts. If the bank failed, how many dollars of his deposit would not be insured?

$

mistakes.why: $250,000 is the amount that is insured. The question asks how much is not: $265,000 − $250,000.
Andre's deposit is insured up to the $250,000 limit; only the amount above the limit is uninsured.

check.hint: Subtract the insurance limit from his deposit.
check.explain: The FDIC limit is $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category. Andre has one individual account, so $250,000 is insured and $265,000 − $250,000 = $15,000 is not.

screens.title: The Federal Reserve
screens.html:
The Federal Reserve ("the Fed") is the central bank of the United States. Congress created it in 1913.

  • It is a bank for banks and for the federal government. Individuals do not open accounts there.
  • It supervises and regulates banks.
  • It conducts monetary policy, mainly by setting a target for short-term interest rates. Congress has directed it to promote maximum employment and stable prices; its long-run goal is about 2 percent inflation a year.

Do not mix up the two agencies. FDIC (1933) = insurance on your deposits. Fed (1913) = central bank and interest rates. The Fed is older; the FDIC came out of the Great Depression.

check.prompt: Which statements about the Federal Reserve are accurate? Select two answers.
options: Congress created it in 1913 as the nation's central bank.
It conducts monetary policy, mainly by influencing interest rates.
It insures each person's savings up to $250,000 per bank.
Individuals can open checking and savings accounts there.
It writes and passes the federal budget each year.
why: That is the FDIC, a different agency created in 1933. The Fed is the central bank, not the deposit insurer.
The Fed serves banks and the federal government. Individuals bank at ordinary banks and credit unions.
Congress passes the budget and the President signs it. Taxing and spending are fiscal policy, not the Fed's job.
check.hint: One statement describes the FDIC and one describes Congress. Which two describe the central bank?
check.explain: The Federal Reserve was created by Congress in 1913 and conducts monetary policy by influencing interest rates. Deposit insurance belongs to the FDIC (1933), and the federal budget belongs to Congress and the President.

screens.title: GDP and Recessions
screens.html:
Gross domestic product (GDP) is the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period, usually a year or a quarter. It is the most common measure of the size of an economy.

Real GDP is adjusted for inflation. If prices rise 5 percent and GDP rises 5 percent, the country did not actually produce more. Real GDP removes the price effect, so it shows whether output truly grew.

When real GDP falls and unemployment rises for a sustained period, the economy is in a recession. Two quarters in a row of falling real GDP is a common rule of thumb; official U.S. recession dates are set by economists at the National Bureau of Economic Research.

To read a GDP graph, compare each bar with the one before it. A shorter bar means the economy shrank.

figure.title: Real GDP of Country P (billions of dollars)

check.prompt: Use the bar graph of Country P. Which statement is supported by the graph?
options: Real GDP fell two years in a row, from Year 2 to Year 4.
Real GDP fell in every year after Year 2.
Real GDP in Year 5 was lower than in Year 1.
Prices in Country P rose fastest in Year 3.
why: Real GDP fell from Year 2 to Year 3 and from Year 3 to Year 4, but it rose from 300 to 318 in Year 5.
Year 5 (318) is higher than Year 1 (300). Compare the two bars directly.
Real GDP is adjusted for inflation, so this graph does not show prices at all.
check.hint: Compare each bar with the one right before it.
check.explain: Real GDP went 312 → 306 → 300 from Year 2 to Year 4, falling two years in a row, then rose to 318 in Year 5. The graph shows real output, not prices, so it cannot support a claim about inflation.

screens.title: Inflation and Percent Change
screens.html:
Inflation is a general rise in the prices of goods and services. When prices rise, each dollar buys less: your purchasing power falls. The Consumer Price Index (CPI), published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, is a common measure of inflation.

Percent change = (new value − old value) ÷ old value × 100

Use this one formula for the inflation rate, GDP growth, or a change in wages. Always divide by the old (starting) value.

If your pay rises more slowly than prices, you can buy less than before, even with a raise. If your pay rises faster than prices, your purchasing power grows.

example.prompt: A basket of household goods cost $80 last year and $84 this year. Your pay rose 3%. What was the inflation rate, and did your purchasing power rise or fall?
steps: Change: $84 − $80 = $4.
Divide by the old price: 4 ÷ 80 = 0.05 = 5%.
Compare: prices rose 5%, pay rose 3%. Prices grew faster.

check.prompt: A price index rose from 240 to 252 in one year. What was the inflation rate for that year? Give your answer as a percent.

mistakes.why: 12 is the change in the index (252 − 240). To get a percent, divide the change by the old value: 12 ÷ 240.
You divided by the new value (12 ÷ 252). Percent change divides by the starting value: 12 ÷ 240.

check.hint: Subtract, divide by the starting value, then multiply by 100.

screens.title: Fiscal Policy and Monetary Policy
screens.html:
The government has two sets of tools to steady the economy. Ask: Who acted, and what tool did they use?

Fiscal policyMonetary policy
Who decidesCongress and the PresidentThe Federal Reserve
ToolsTaxes and government spendingInterest rates and the money supply
To boost a weak economyCut taxes or increase spendingLower interest rates
To cool high inflationRaise taxes or cut spendingRaise interest rates

The Constitution gives Congress the power to tax and spend, and says all bills for raising revenue must start in the House of Representatives (Article I, Section 7). When the Fed raises interest rates, loans cost more, so people and businesses borrow and spend less, which eases pressure on prices.

screens.title: Reading Economic Viewpoints
screens.html:
Economists and political leaders often disagree about when and how the government should act. Some stress acting quickly to protect jobs; others stress long-term costs, such as a larger national debt or higher inflation. GED questions do not ask which side is right. They ask you to:

  • Identify each speaker's main point and the tool they favor (taxes and spending, or interest rates)
  • Find the evidence each side uses
  • Separate facts (can be checked with records or data) from opinions (judgments people can disagree with)

Opinion signals: best, worst, should, clearly, foolish, wise, unfair, greatest. A sentence that reports what someone said can still be a fact: "The senator said the plan is unwise" is a checkable fact about what was said.

check.prompt: Read the short news report. Click the sentence that expresses an opinion rather than a fact that could be checked.
spans: Last week the Federal Reserve raised its target interest rate by one-quarter of a percentage point.
It was the third increase this year.
Consumer prices rose 4.1 percent over the past twelve months, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Raising rates again was a reckless choice that will hurt working families more than it helps them.
The Fed's next scheduled meeting is in six weeks.
check.why: Some students click the inflation sentence because it sounds like an argument for the rate increase, but a published price statistic can be checked. The judgment “a reckless choice” cannot be proved true or false.
check.hint: Which sentence uses a judgment word that people could reasonably disagree with?
check.explain: "Raising rates again was a reckless choice that will hurt working families more than it helps them" is a judgment: "reckless" is an opinion word, and the claim about who is helped more is a prediction people could dispute. The rate change, the count of increases, the price statistic, and the meeting date can all be checked in records.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• Scarcity: unlimited wants, limited resources, so every choice has a trade-off. Opportunity cost = the next best alternative only.
  • Factors of production: land, labor, capital (tools and machines), entrepreneurship.
  • Law of demand: price up, quantity demanded down. Law of supply: price up, quantity supplied up.
  • Equilibrium: demanded = supplied. Below it, a shortage; above it, a surplus. Size = larger − smaller.
  • Shifts: buyers' events shift demand; sellers' events shift supply. Ceiling below equilibrium → shortage; floor above → surplus.
  • Systems: market, command, mixed (United States). Competition lowers prices; a monopoly has no rivals. Sherman Antitrust Act (1890).
  • Money: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value. FDIC (1933): $250,000 insurance. Fed (1913): central bank, interest rates.
  • GDP measures output; real GDP is adjusted for inflation. Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
  • Fiscal = Congress and the President, taxes and spending. Monetary = the Fed, interest rates.

stimuli.title: When a Second Provider Came to Town
stimuli.html:
For more than ten years, Northline Cable was the only company that offered home internet service in the small town of Harlow. Its basic plan cost $85 a month for a speed of 100 megabits per second (Mbps). Residents who were unhappy with the price or the service had nowhere else to go.

In 2023, a second company, Valley Fiber, finished laying new lines and began selling service in Harlow. Valley Fiber offered 300 Mbps for $55 a month. Within a year, Northline lowered the price of its basic plan to $60 a month and raised its speed to 300 Mbps. Northline also dropped a $10 monthly equipment fee that it had charged for years.

Economists call a market with only one seller and no close substitutes a monopoly. Being the only seller is not illegal by itself. However, federal antitrust laws, beginning with the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, make it illegal for companies to agree with competitors to fix prices or to use unfair tactics to create or keep a monopoly.

stimuli.title: How Banks and the Federal Reserve Work
stimuli.html:
A bank is a business. It accepts deposits from customers and pays them interest, and it lends money to other customers who pay interest on their loans. A bank might pay 1 percent interest on a savings account and charge 7 percent on a car loan. The difference between the interest a bank earns on loans and the interest it pays on deposits is a major source of its profit. Banks keep only part of their deposits on hand; much of the rest is lent out.

Because banks lend out deposits, a bank can fail if many loans go unpaid or if too many depositors try to withdraw their money at once. Thousands of banks failed in the early years of the Great Depression, and many families lost their savings. In response, Congress created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) in 1933. Today, the FDIC insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category. If an insured bank fails, depositors get their insured money back.

The Federal Reserve, created by Congress in 1913, is the central bank of the United States. Individuals do not open accounts there; it serves banks and the federal government. The Federal Reserve supervises banks and conducts monetary policy, mainly by influencing short-term interest rates. Congress has directed it to promote maximum employment and stable prices.
stimuli.source: Summary written for this lesson; facts from the FDIC and the Federal Reserve

stimuli.title: Two Views on Government Action in a Recession
stimuli.html:
Economist A: When a recession hits, families and businesses cut back on spending. That drop in demand leads businesses to lay off workers, who then spend even less. During a recession, the federal government should step in by increasing spending on projects such as road and bridge repair or by cutting taxes for a limited time. Putting money into the economy can help businesses keep workers until conditions improve.

Economist B: When the federal government spends more than it collects in taxes, it must borrow the difference, and that borrowing adds to the national debt. Future taxpayers will have to pay interest on that debt. Large spending increases can also be slow to take effect. Instead, the Federal Reserve can lower interest rates, which encourages people and businesses to borrow and spend without adding to the national debt.

stimuli.title: A Second Grocery Store in Millbrook
stimuli.html:
For eight years, FreshWay was the only grocery store in Millbrook, a town of about 9,000 people. Residents who wanted to shop somewhere else had to drive 25 miles. FreshWay closed at 8 p.m. and offered no delivery.

In 2022, a regional discount chain, ValuMart, opened a store across town. ValuMart's prices on common items such as milk, eggs, and bread were about 15 percent lower than FreshWay's. Within six months, FreshWay cut prices on 400 common items, began staying open until 10 p.m., and started a free delivery service for older residents. FreshWay's manager told the local newspaper, "We had to give people a reason to keep shopping with us."

Economists explain that when buyers can choose among sellers, each seller has a reason to lower prices or improve service. A company that wins customers this way breaks no law. Federal antitrust laws, however, forbid competitors from agreeing with each other to set prices.

stimuli.title: Money, Barter, and Banks
stimuli.html:
Imagine a farmer who wants a pair of shoes. Without money, she must find a shoemaker who has shoes to trade and who also wants what she has, such as eggs. This kind of direct trade is called barter, and it is slow and difficult. Money solves the problem. Because everyone accepts it, money serves as a medium of exchange. It also serves as a unit of account, since prices are stated in dollars, and as a store of value, since it can be saved and spent later.

Most of the money Americans use today is not paper bills or coins but balances in bank accounts. When a customer deposits $1,000, the bank keeps part of it on hand and lends much of the rest to borrowers, who pay interest. The bank pays its depositors a lower rate of interest than it charges borrowers.

Money works well as a store of value only when prices are fairly stable. If prices rise 4 percent in a year, $100 kept in a drawer buys about 4 percent less at the end of the year. To keep inflation low and steady, the Federal Reserve adjusts its target interest rate. Separately, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) insures bank deposits so that customers do not lose insured savings if a bank fails.

stimuli.title: Two Views on Fighting Inflation
stimuli.html:
Economist C: Prices have risen more than 5 percent a year for over a year. Inflation this high shrinks the value of workers' paychecks and families' savings. The Federal Reserve should raise interest rates quickly and keep them high until inflation returns to its 2 percent goal. If it waits, people and businesses will start to expect high inflation every year, and that expectation makes inflation much harder to stop.

Economist D: I agree that inflation must come down, but higher interest rates take many months to work their way through the economy. If the Federal Reserve raises rates too far, too fast, businesses may cut jobs and the economy could slip into a recession. The Fed should raise rates in small steps and study the data before each move. Congress could also help by slowing the growth of federal spending.

items.prompt: Andre has $40 left after paying his bills this week. He could buy new work boots, buy a ticket to a basketball game, or put the money in savings. He buys the boots. He says that if he had not bought the boots, he would have gone to the game. What is the opportunity cost of buying the boots?
options: The basketball game ticket
The new work boots
The basketball game ticket plus the money he could have saved
The $40 put into savings
why: The boots are what Andre chose. Opportunity cost is what he gave up to get them.
You added two options together. Andre could spend the $40 only once, so only his next best choice counts.
Saving ranked third on his list. He says the game is what he would have picked instead.
items.hint: Opportunity cost is the next best choice, the one he would have picked instead.
items.explain:
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up. Andre says that without the boots he would have gone to the game, so the game ticket is his next best choice and his opportunity cost.

The boots are what he chose, not what he gave up. Adding the game and savings together is wrong because he could only use the $40 once. Savings ranked third on his list, not second.

items.prompt: Based on the table, at what price does the quantity of kayak rentals demanded equal the quantity supplied?
why: At $15, 75 rentals are demanded but only 45 are supplied. The numbers do not match; that row shows a shortage.

At $30, 90 are supplied and 30 demanded, a large surplus. Equilibrium is where the two quantities are equal.
items.hint: Look for the row where the two quantity columns show the same number.
items.explain:
At $20, quantity demanded is 60 and quantity supplied is 60. Because they are equal, $20 is the equilibrium price. On the graph, this is where the two lines cross.

At $15, 75 are demanded but only 45 supplied (a shortage). At $25, 75 are supplied but only 45 demanded (a surplus). At $30, the surplus is even larger.

items.hint: Find the $30 row. Subtract quantity demanded from quantity supplied.
items.explain:
At $30:
Quantity supplied = 90

Surplus = 90 − 30 = 60 rentals per day.

items.prompt: Each event below affects the market for coffee. Drag each event into the box that shows how it changes the market for coffee.
choices: A widely reported health study finds that drinking coffee improves memory.
A frost destroys a large share of the coffee crop in a major growing region.
The price of tea, a substitute for coffee, falls sharply.
A new machine lets coffee farms harvest beans faster and at lower cost.
The government places a new tax on coffee producers for every pound they sell.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the frost under “Demand decreases.” Buyers still want coffee; the frost hits growers, so it decreases supply. Cheaper tea is the other trap: tea is a substitute, so cheaper tea pulls buyers away from coffee.
items.hint: First ask whether the event affects buyers (demand) or sellers (supply). Then decide the direction.
items.explain:
• Health study: changes buyers' tastes; more people want coffee. Demand increases.
  • Frost: farmers can produce less. Supply decreases.
  • Cheaper tea: tea is a substitute, so some coffee drinkers switch to tea. Demand for coffee decreases.
  • New machine: better technology lowers costs, so sellers can offer more. Supply increases.
  • Tax on producers: raises sellers' costs. Supply decreases.

A common error is putting the frost under "demand decreases." Buyers still want coffee; there is simply less to sell.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?

Northline broke the Sherman Antitrust Act by being Harlow's only internet provider.

Internet prices in every town fell in 2023, whether or not a new company arrived.
why: The passage says being the only seller "is not illegal by itself." It never says Northline fixed prices or used unfair tactics.
The passage says nothing about Valley Fiber's future. This is a prediction the text does not support.
The passage describes only Harlow. It gives no information about prices in other towns.
items.hint: What did Northline change, and what happened just before it changed?
items.explain:
After Valley Fiber entered the market with a cheaper, faster plan, Northline cut its price from $85 to $60, tripled its speed from 100 to 300 Mbps, and dropped a $10 fee. This supports the conclusion that competition led Northline to offer a better deal.

The passage says that being the only seller "is not illegal by itself," so it does not support the claim that Northline broke the law. Nothing in the passage predicts Valley Fiber's future or describes prices in other towns.

items.prompt: Which statements are supported by the passage? Select two answers.
options: Banks earn money partly by charging borrowers a higher interest rate than they pay depositors.

Individuals can open savings accounts directly at the Federal Reserve.
Banks keep all of their customers' deposits in their vaults at all times.
Congress created the Federal Reserve in response to bank failures during the Great Depression.
why: The passage says individuals "do not open accounts" at the Federal Reserve; it serves banks and the government.
The passage says banks "keep only part of their deposits on hand" and lend much of the rest.
Check the dates. The Federal Reserve was created in 1913, before the Depression. The agency created after Depression-era bank failures was the FDIC (1933).
items.hint: Check each statement against the passage. Watch the dates: which agency was created in 1913 and which in 1933?
items.explain:
Correct: The passage says the difference between the interest a bank earns on loans and the interest it pays on deposits "is a major source of its profit," and that the FDIC insures deposits up to $250,000 so that depositors "get their insured money back."

Incorrect: The passage says individuals "do not open accounts" at the Federal Reserve, and that banks "keep only part of their deposits on hand." The Federal Reserve was created in 1913, before the Great Depression; the agency created in response to Depression-era bank failures was the FDIC (1933).

options: raises

items.explain:
Fiscal policy is the use of taxes and spending. It is set by Congress and the President through laws and the federal budget. Monetary policy is the management of interest rates and the money supply by the Federal Reserve. To fight high inflation, the Fed usually raises interest rates; higher rates make loans more expensive, so people and businesses borrow and spend less, which eases the pressure on prices.

A common error is choosing "the Federal Reserve" for the second blank. The Fed controls monetary policy, not taxes or spending.

items.prompt: According to the graph, between which two years did Country Z's real GDP decrease?
options: Year 1 to Year 2
Year 2 to Year 3
Year 3 to Year 4
Year 4 to Year 5
why: Real GDP rose from 640 to 662. A taller bar means growth, not a decrease.
Real GDP rose from 662 to 681. Compare each bar with the one right after it.
Year 4 is the low point, but GDP rose after it, from 655 to 668. The drop happened just before Year 4.
items.hint: Compare each bar with the one right after it. Which bar is shorter than the bar before it?
