Real GDP values: Year 1, 640; Year 2, 662; Year 3, 681; Year 4, 655; Year 5, 668; Year 6, 700 (billions of dollars).

From Year 3 to Year 4, real GDP fell from 681 to 655, a drop of 681 − 655 = 26 billion dollars. Every other pair of years shows an increase. Because real GDP is adjusted for inflation, this drop means the country actually produced less, which is a sign of a recession.

Year 4 to Year 5 is a common wrong choice: Year 4 is the low point, but GDP rose from 655 to 668 after it.

items.prompt: In the fictional nation of Korvia, a national planning board decides how many cars, shoes, and loaves of bread factories will make each year. The board also sets the price of every product, and private businesses are not allowed. Which kind of economic system does Korvia have?
options: A command economy
A market economy
A mixed economy
An oligopoly
why: In a market economy, buyers and sellers decide what is made and at what price. In Korvia, a government board decides both.
A mixed economy has mostly private businesses plus some government rules. Korvia allows no private businesses at all.
An oligopoly is one market with a few large sellers, not a whole economic system run by a planning board.
items.hint: Who decides what is produced and what it costs?
items.explain: Every economy must decide what to produce, how, and for whom. In Korvia, a government planning board makes those decisions and sets prices, which is a command economy. A mixed economy, like that of the United States, is tempting because it also includes government, but in a mixed economy private businesses make most decisions.

items.prompt: Dana's hourly wage rose from $20.00 in Year 2 to $20.60 in Year 3. Based on the table, which statement best describes what happened to Dana's purchasing power from Year 2 to Year 3?
options: It fell, because her wage rose 3% while the cost of the basket rose 5%.
It fell, because her wage rose 3% while the cost of the basket rose 4%.
It rose, because her wage went up by $0.60 an hour.
It stayed the same, because both her wage and prices went up.
why: You compared her wage with the Year 1 to Year 2 change in the basket (500 to 520 = 4%). The question asks about Year 2 to Year 3: 520 to 546 = 5%.
A raise in dollars does not by itself raise purchasing power. Compare her 3% raise with the 5% rise in prices.
Both rose, but by different amounts. Prices rose 5% and her wage only 3%, so each hour of work buys less.
items.hint: Find the percent change in her wage and the percent change in the basket's total cost from Year 2 to Year 3, then compare.
items.explain:
Wage change: $20.60 − $20.00 = $0.60; 0.60 ÷ 20.00 = 0.03 = 3%.

Price change (Year 2 to Year 3): $546 − $520 = $26; 26 ÷ 520 = 0.05 = 5%.

Prices rose faster than her pay (5% > 3%), so each hour of work buys less than before. Her purchasing power fell.

The 4% choice uses the wrong years: from Year 1 to Year 2, the basket rose from $500 to $520, and 20 ÷ 500 = 4%. A raise in dollars does not mean higher purchasing power if prices rise faster.

items.prompt: Read the news brief below about the fictional city of Riverton. Click the sentence that expresses an opinion rather than a fact that could be checked.
spans: On Tuesday, the Riverton City Council voted 5 to 2 to raise the standard bus fare from $1.50 to $2.00 beginning March 1.
According to the transit agency's annual report, the cost of running the bus system rose 18 percent over the past three years.
Fares currently cover about one-fourth of the system's operating costs, and the rest comes from city and federal funds.
Council Member Ruth Okafor, who voted no, pointed out that ridership dropped after the last fare increase.
Any city that raises bus fares during hard times has clearly forgotten the riders who depend on buses the most.
The transit agency will hold two public hearings in February to explain the change.
items.why: Many students click Council Member Okafor's sentence because it disagrees with the fare increase. But it reports what she pointed out, and ridership records can be checked. The judgment “has clearly forgotten the riders” is the opinion.
items.hint: A fact can be proved true or false with records or data. An opinion is a judgment that people could reasonably disagree with.
items.explain:
The sentence "Any city that raises bus fares during hard times has clearly forgotten the riders who depend on buses the most" is a judgment. Words such as "clearly forgotten" signal the writer's belief, and no record could prove it true or false.

The other sentences can be checked: the council vote and new fare are public record, the cost increase and funding shares come from the agency's report, the hearings are scheduled events, and what Council Member Okafor said is a fact about her statement (and ridership numbers can be checked).

items.skill: Predicting effects of a price ceiling
items.prompt: Suppose the Pine Lake town council sets a maximum price of $15 per kayak rental. Based on the table, what would most likely result?
options: A shortage of 30 rentals per day
A surplus of 30 rentals per day
A shortage of 60 rentals per day
75 rentals per day, enough for every customer who wants one
why: A legal maximum below equilibrium holds the price too low. At $15, demanded (75) is bigger than supplied (45), so it is a shortage, not a surplus.
That is the gap at $10 (90 − 30). The ceiling is $15, so use the $15 row: 75 − 45.
75 is how many rentals customers want at $15. Businesses would offer only 45, so 30 customers a day would go without.
items.hint: Find the $15 row. Compare how many rentals customers want with how many businesses offer.
items.explain:
A legal maximum price is a price ceiling. Here it is below the equilibrium price of $20, so the price will settle at $15.

At $15:
Quantity demanded = 75
Quantity supplied = 45
Demanded is greater, so there is a shortage: 75 − 45 = 30 rentals per day.

A shortage of 60 comes from reading the $10 row. The 75-rental choice is wrong because businesses would offer only 45 rentals at $15, so 30 customers a day would go without.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the main difference between the two economists?
options: Economist A favors using fiscal policy to fight a recession, while Economist B worries about its long-term cost and prefers monetary policy.
Economist A wants the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, while Economist B wants Congress to cut taxes.
Economist A believes recessions are caused by the national debt, while Economist B believes they are caused by low interest rates.
Economist A argues that government should take no action in a recession, while Economist B argues that Congress should spend more.
why: This reverses the tools. Neither economist wants higher interest rates, and Economist A is the one who supports tax cuts and spending.
Neither economist explains what causes recessions. Both describe what to do during one.
Economist A favors government action (more spending or tax cuts), and it is Economist B who warns about new spending.
items.hint: Identify which tool each economist recommends: taxes and spending, or interest rates.
items.explain:
Economist A recommends higher government spending or temporary tax cuts: these are fiscal policy tools. Economist B warns that borrowing adds to the national debt and that spending can be slow, and recommends that the Federal Reserve lower interest rates: a monetary policy tool. So A favors fiscal policy, and B is concerned about its costs and prefers monetary policy.

The other choices reverse or invent positions. Neither economist wants higher interest rates, neither explains what causes recessions, and it is B, not A, who is cautious about new spending. The question asks you to describe the viewpoints, not decide which one is right.

items.prompt: Based on the table, by what percent did the total monthly cost of the basket rise from Year 1 to Year 3? Give your answer as a percent.

mistakes.why: $46 is the dollar increase ($546 − $500). To get a percent, divide by the Year 1 total: 46 ÷ 500.
That is the rise from Year 2 to Year 3 only. The question asks about Year 1 to Year 3: $500 to $546.
You divided by the Year 3 total (46 ÷ 546). Percent change divides by the starting value, $500.

items.hint: Use the Total row. Subtract, divide by the Year 1 total, then multiply by 100.
items.explain:
Year 1 total: $500. Year 3 total: $546.
Change: $546 − $500 = $46
Divide by the starting value: 46 ÷ 500 = 0.092
Convert: 0.092 × 100 = 9.2%

A common error is dividing by $546, the new value, which gives about 8.4%.

items.prompt: Lena owns a small bakery and has $5,000 to invest this year. She could buy a second oven, run an online advertising campaign, or pay down a business loan. She buys the oven. She says that if she had not bought the oven, she would have run the advertising campaign. What is the opportunity cost of buying the oven?
options: The online advertising campaign
The second oven
The ad campaign plus paying down the loan
Paying down the business loan
why: The oven is what Lena chose. Opportunity cost is what she gave up to get it.
You added two options together. Lena could spend the $5,000 only once, so only her next best choice counts.
Paying down the loan ranked third on her list. She says the ad campaign is what she would have picked instead.
items.hint: Which option does Lena say she would have chosen instead?
items.explain: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up. Lena says she would have run the ad campaign, so the advertising campaign is her opportunity cost. Adding the loan payment is wrong because she could use the $5,000 only once, and the oven is what she gained, not what she gave up.

items.prompt: Based on the table, at what price per gallon does the quantity of milk demanded equal the quantity supplied?
why: At $3.50, 8,200 gallons are demanded but only 5,400 are supplied. The numbers do not match; that row shows a shortage.
At $4.50, 8,600 gallons are supplied but only 5,800 are demanded. That row shows a surplus.
At $5.00, 10,200 are supplied and 4,600 demanded, a large surplus. Equilibrium is where the two quantities are equal.
items.hint: Look for the row where the two quantity columns show the same number.
items.explain: At $4.00, quantity demanded is 7,000 gallons and quantity supplied is 7,000 gallons. Because they are equal, $4.00 is the equilibrium price. On the graph, it is where the two lines cross. Prices below $4.00 give shortages, and prices above it give surpluses.

items.prompt: If milk were priced at $3.50 a gallon, how many more gallons per week would shoppers want than sellers would offer?

mistakes.why: That is the gap at $3.00 (9,400 − 3,800). Use the $3.50 row: 8,200 − 5,400.
You added the two quantities (8,200 + 5,400). The size of a shortage is the difference between them.

items.hint: Find the $3.50 row. Subtract quantity supplied from quantity demanded.
items.explain:
At $3.50:
Quantity demanded = 8,200
Quantity supplied = 5,400
Shortage = 8,200 − 5,400 = 2,800 gallons per week.

A common error is reading the $3.00 row, which gives 5,600.

items.prompt: Each event below affects the market for hamburger buns. Drag each event into the box that shows how it changes the market for hamburger buns.
choices: Ground beef prices jump sharply as cattle herds shrink.
A summer heat wave sparks a nationwide surge in backyard cookouts.
A bakery chain installs new ovens that bake twice as many buns per hour.
The price of flour, the main ingredient in buns, rises steeply.
A fire shuts down the region's largest bun factory for three months.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the ground beef event under a supply box. Beef is not an input for buns; it is a complement used together with them, so pricier beef means people buy fewer burgers and fewer buns. That lowers demand for buns.
items.hint: First ask whether the event affects buyers (demand) or bakers (supply). Then decide the direction.
items.explain:
• Ground beef prices jump: beef and buns are complements (used together). Fewer burgers means fewer buns wanted. Demand decreases.
  • Heat wave and cookouts: buyers want more buns. Demand increases.
  • New ovens: better technology lowers costs, so bakers offer more. Supply increases.
  • Flour costs more: an input cost rises, so bakers offer less. Supply decreases.
  • Factory fire: fewer buns can be made. Supply decreases.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: FreshWay lowered prices and improved service after a competitor opened in town.
FreshWay broke federal antitrust law by being Millbrook's only grocery for eight years.
ValuMart and FreshWay agreed with each other to set the prices of milk, eggs, and bread.
Grocery prices fell in every town where ValuMart opened a new store in 2022.
why: The passage says a company that wins customers by competing "breaks no law," and nothing says FreshWay fixed prices or used unfair tactics.
Nothing in the passage describes an agreement between the stores. FreshWay changed its prices after ValuMart charged less, which is competition, not price fixing.
The passage describes only Millbrook. It gives no information about other towns where ValuMart opened.
items.hint: What did FreshWay change, and what happened just before it changed?
items.explain:
After ValuMart opened with prices about 15 percent lower, FreshWay cut prices on 400 items, stayed open two hours later, and started free delivery. Its manager said, "We had to give people a reason to keep shopping with us." This supports the conclusion that competition led FreshWay to lower prices and improve service.

Being the only store was not described as illegal, and the passage never mentions an agreement between the stores or prices in other towns.

items.prompt: Which statements are supported by the passage? Select two answers.
options: Barter requires each trader to find someone who has what they want and wants what they have.
When prices rise, money that has been saved can buy less than before.
Banks keep every deposited dollar on hand so that customers can withdraw it at any time.
Most of the money Americans use today is in the form of paper bills and coins.
The FDIC adjusts its target interest rate to keep inflation low and steady.
why: The passage says the bank "keeps part of it on hand and lends much of the rest."
The passage says most money today is "not paper bills or coins but balances in bank accounts."
The passage says the Federal Reserve adjusts its target interest rate. The FDIC insures deposits.
items.hint: Check each statement against the exact words of the passage. Watch which agency does what.
items.explain:
Correct: The farmer example shows that barter requires finding someone who has what you want and wants what you have. The passage also says that if prices rise 4 percent, $100 "buys about 4 percent less," so saved money loses buying power.

Incorrect: Banks keep only "part" of deposits on hand; most money today is bank balances, not cash; and it is the Federal Reserve, not the FDIC, that adjusts interest rates.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements.

To help slow high inflation, Congress could {{0}} federal spending. That choice would be an example of {{1}} policy. At the same time, the Federal Reserve could {{2}} its target interest rate, which would make loans {{3}}.

options: cut
increase
double
why: More government spending adds money to the economy, which would push prices up, not slow inflation.
Doubling spending would pour more money into the economy and add to inflation pressure.

options: fiscal
monetary
antitrust
trade
why: Monetary policy is the Federal Reserve's tool (interest rates). Congress changing spending is fiscal policy.
Antitrust policy deals with competition and monopolies, not the federal budget.
Trade policy deals with imports, exports, and tariffs, not overall federal spending.

options: raise
lower
eliminate
why: Lower rates make borrowing cheaper and encourage spending, which would add to inflation, not slow it.
The Fed changes its target rate up or down; to cool inflation it raises the rate.

options: more expensive
cheaper
tax-free
why: Higher interest rates mean borrowers pay more interest, so loans get more expensive, not cheaper.
Interest rates do not make loans tax-free; they change how much borrowing costs.

items.hint: Which actions take money out of the economy? Congress uses spending; the Fed uses interest rates.
items.explain: To slow inflation, Congress could cut spending, which is fiscal policy because it uses the federal budget. The Federal Reserve could raise its target rate, making loans more expensive, so people and businesses borrow and spend less. A common error is calling the spending cut "monetary" because it involves money; fiscal policy is any change in taxes or spending by Congress and the President.

items.prompt: According to the graph, during which period did Country R's real GDP fall for two quarters in a row?
options: Q1 to Q3
Q2 to Q4
Q3 to Q5
Q4 to Q6
why: From Q1 to Q2, real GDP rose (410 to 418) before falling to 412. That is only one quarter of decline.
Real GDP fell from Q3 to Q4 (412 to 405), but then rose to 409 in Q5. That is only one quarter of decline.
Real GDP rose in both quarters (405 to 409 to 421). This is the recovery, not a decline.
items.hint: Trace the line from point to point. Where does it go down twice in a row?
items.explain:
Real GDP values: Q1, 410; Q2, 418; Q3, 412; Q4, 405; Q5, 409; Q6, 421 (billions of dollars).

From Q2 to Q3 it fell (418 to 412), and from Q3 to Q4 it fell again (412 to 405): two quarters in a row. Two straight quarters of falling real GDP is a common rule-of-thumb sign of a recession. Q3 to Q5 is the tempting wrong choice, but GDP rose from Q4 to Q5.

items.prompt: Adam Smith wrote that in a market, people pursuing their own interests are guided "as if by an invisible hand" to meet the needs of others. Which situation is the best example of this idea?
options: Bakers in a town start making gluten-free bread after customers begin asking for it, with no government order.
A national planning board orders clothing factories to produce 10,000 more winter coats this year.
Congress votes to lower income taxes so that families will have more money to spend.
Three airlines secretly agree to charge the same fare so that none of them loses customers.
why: A planning board giving orders is a command economy. The invisible hand works through buyers' and sellers' own choices, without orders.
A tax cut by Congress is fiscal policy, a government decision. The invisible hand describes private market choices.
Secretly fixing prices blocks the market from working and is illegal under antitrust law. The invisible hand depends on competition.
items.hint: The invisible hand works through prices and private choices, not government orders or secret deals.
items.explain: In the bakery example, sellers chase their own profit by making what customers want, and customers' needs get met without anyone giving orders. That is Adam Smith's invisible hand and the core of a market economy. The planning board is a command economy, the tax cut is fiscal policy, and the airline agreement is price fixing.

items.prompt: By how many billion dollars did Country R's real GDP fall from Q2 to Q4?

mistakes.why: That is only the drop from Q2 to Q3 (418 − 412). The question asks about Q2 to Q4: 418 − 405.
That is only the drop from Q3 to Q4 (412 − 405). Start at Q2: 418 − 405.

items.hint: Read the Q2 and Q4 points, then subtract.
items.explain:
Q2: 418 billion dollars
Q4: 405 billion dollars
Change: 418 − 405 = 13 billion dollars.

You can check it in two steps: 6 (Q2 to Q3) + 7 (Q3 to Q4) = 13.

items.prompt: Marcus's monthly take-home pay rose from $2,500 in Year 2 to $2,600 in Year 3. Based on the table, which statement best describes what happened to Marcus's purchasing power from Year 2 to Year 3?
options: It rose, because his pay rose 4% while the cost of the basket rose 2%.
It fell, because his pay rose 4% while the cost of the basket rose 5%.
It fell, because the total cost of the basket went up by $21 a month.
It stayed the same, because both his pay and prices went up that year.
why: You used the wrong years. The basket rose 5% from Year 1 to Year 2 ($1,000 to $1,050). From Year 2 to Year 3 it rose from $1,050 to $1,071, which is 2%.
Rising prices alone do not mean purchasing power fell. Compare the percent changes: pay up 4%, prices up 2%.
Both rose, but by different amounts. Pay rose 4% and prices only 2%, so his pay buys more than before.
items.hint: Find the percent change in his pay and in the basket's total cost from Year 2 to Year 3, then compare.
items.explain:
Pay change: $2,600 − $2,500 = $100; 100 ÷ 2,500 = 0.04 = 4%.

Price change (Year 2 to Year 3): $1,071 − $1,050 = $21; 21 ÷ 1,050 = 0.02 = 2%.

Pay rose faster than prices (4% > 2%), so Marcus's purchasing power rose.

The 5% choice uses Year 1 to Year 2 ($50 ÷ $1,000). Rising prices do not lower purchasing power if pay rises faster.

items.prompt: Read the news brief below about the fictional county of Fairview. Click the sentence that expresses an opinion rather than a fact that could be checked.
spans: On Monday, the Fairview County Commission voted 4 to 1 to add a 5-cent tax to each gallon of gasoline sold in the county.
According to the county budget office, the tax is expected to raise about $3 million a year for road repairs.
Gas stations in two neighboring counties now charge an average of 8 cents less per gallon than Fairview stations.
Commissioner Lee Ortiz, who voted against the tax, said some drivers may cross the county line to buy cheaper gas.
Making drivers pay even more at the pump is the worst possible way to fix the county's roads.
The new tax takes effect on July 1.
items.why: Many students click Commissioner Ortiz's sentence because it criticizes the tax. But it reports what he said, which is a checkable fact. “The worst possible way” is the writer's own judgment.
items.hint: A fact can be proved true or false with records or data. Look for a judgment word.
items.explain:
"Making drivers pay even more at the pump is the worst possible way to fix the county's roads" is a judgment. "The worst possible way" signals the writer's belief, and no record could prove it.

The vote count, the revenue estimate, the price comparison, what Commissioner Ortiz said, and the start date can all be checked.

items.skill: Predicting effects of a price floor
items.prompt: Suppose a new law sets a minimum price of $5.00 per gallon of milk in Dale County. Based on the table, what would most likely result?
options: A surplus of 5,600 gallons per week
A shortage of 5,600 gallons per week
A surplus of 2,800 gallons per week
10,200 gallons sold per week, the amount sellers offer
why: A legal minimum above equilibrium holds the price too high. At $5.00, supplied (10,200) is bigger than demanded (4,600), so it is a surplus, not a shortage.
That is the gap at $4.50 (8,600 − 5,800). The minimum price is $5.00, so use the $5.00 row.
Sellers would offer 10,200 gallons, but shoppers would buy only 4,600. You cannot sell more than buyers want, so the extra goes unsold.
items.hint: A legal minimum price is a price floor. Find the $5.00 row and compare the two quantities.
items.explain:
A legal minimum price is a price floor. Here it is above the equilibrium price of $4.00, so the price stays at $5.00.

At $5.00:
Quantity supplied = 10,200
Quantity demanded = 4,600
Supplied is greater, so there is a surplus: 10,200 − 4,600 = 5,600 gallons per week.

Only 4,600 gallons would actually be sold, because shoppers want only that many at $5.00.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the main difference between the two economists?
options: Both want higher interest rates, but Economist C wants large, fast increases and Economist D wants small, careful steps.
Economist C wants the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, while Economist D wants it to lower rates to protect jobs.
Economist C wants Congress to cut federal spending, while Economist D wants the Federal Reserve to act on its own.
Economist C believes inflation does little harm, while Economist D believes it must be brought down.
why: Economist D says the Fed "should raise rates in small steps." D worries about raising too fast, but never asks for lower rates.
This reverses the two views. Economist D is the one who mentions Congress slowing spending; Economist C talks only about the Federal Reserve.
Economist C says inflation "shrinks the value of workers' paychecks and families' savings," and Economist D agrees it "must come down."
items.hint: Do they agree on the direction of interest rates? What do they disagree about?
items.explain:
Both economists want inflation to come down and both favor raising interest rates. Economist C wants the Fed to raise rates "quickly" and keep them high, warning that waiting lets people expect high inflation. Economist D wants "small steps," warning that raising rates too fast could cause job losses and a recession. The difference is speed and size, not direction.

The choice saying D wants lower rates is the trap: D is cautious but still says to raise rates. The question asks you to describe the views, not decide which is right.

items.prompt: Based on the table, by what percent did the total monthly cost of the basket rise from Year 1 to Year 3? Give your answer as a percent.

mistakes.why: $71 is the dollar increase ($1,071 − $1,000). To get a percent, divide by the Year 1 total: 71 ÷ 1,000.
That is the rise from Year 2 to Year 3 only. The question asks about Year 1 to Year 3: $1,000 to $1,071.
You divided by the Year 3 total (71 ÷ 1,071). Percent change divides by the starting value, $1,000.

items.hint: Use the Total row. Subtract, divide by the Year 1 total, then multiply by 100.
items.explain:
Year 1 total: $1,000. Year 3 total: $1,071.
Change: $1,071 − $1,000 = $71
Divide by the starting value: 71 ÷ 1,000 = 0.071
Convert: 0.071 × 100 = 7.1%

A common error is dividing by $1,071, the new value, which gives about 6.6%.

items.prompt: Renee has three ways to spend Saturday: a $90 shift at her regular job, a $120 catering job across the county, or her nephew's birthday party. She works the $90 shift. She says that if she had not worked the shift, she would have gone to the party, because the catering job was too far to drive. What is the opportunity cost of working the shift?
options: Going to her nephew's birthday party
The $120 catering job, since it paid the most
The catering job and the party together
Nothing, since the shift earned her $90
why: Opportunity cost is the option the person would actually have chosen next, not the one with the biggest dollar amount. Renee ruled out the catering job.
You added two options together. Renee could spend Saturday only one way, so only her next best choice counts.
The $90 is what she gained. Every choice has an opportunity cost: what she gave up to work the shift.
items.explain: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up. Renee says that without the shift she would have gone to the party, so that is her opportunity cost. The $120 catering job is the trap: it pays the most, but Renee says she would not have taken it, so it was not her next best choice.

items.prompt: At a price of $30 per month, how many more memberships would Oakdale residents want than gyms would offer?

mistakes.why: That is the gap at $20 (1,500 − 500). Use the $30 row: 1,300 − 800.
You added the two quantities (1,300 + 800). The size of a shortage is the difference between them.

items.explain:
At $30:
Quantity demanded = 1,300
Quantity supplied = 800
Demanded is bigger, so there is a shortage: 1,300 − 800 = 500 memberships.

items.prompt: A new manufacturing method cuts the cost of producing solar panels by 30 percent. What will most likely happen in the market for solar panels?
options: Supply increases, so the price falls and more panels are sold.
Supply decreases, so the price rises and fewer panels are sold.
Demand increases, so the price rises and more panels are sold.
Supply increases, so the price falls and fewer panels are sold.
why: Lower production costs let sellers offer more, not less. A cost increase would decrease supply.
The new method affects the companies that make panels, not buyers' wants. That is a supply event, and more supply lowers the price.
The supply shift and price drop are right, but a lower price leads buyers to purchase more panels, not fewer.
items.explain: Buyers or sellers? The new method lowers sellers' costs, so this is a supply event. Direction: cheaper production means sellers offer more, so supply increases. Result: the price falls, and at the lower price buyers purchase more panels. Calling it a demand increase is the common error: buyers did not change what they want.

items.prompt: For ten years, Marlow's Cafe was the only coffee shop on Grant Street. This year, three new coffee shops opened on the same block. Based on how competition works, which outcome is most likely?
options: Marlow's Cafe lowers some prices or improves its service to keep its customers.
Marlow's Cafe raises its prices to make up for the customers it has lost.
The city government sets one price for all coffee sold on Grant Street.
Marlow's Cafe becomes a monopoly because it has been there the longest.
why: With rivals nearby, customers can switch if Marlow's charges more. Competition pushes prices down, not up.
In a market economy, sellers set their own prices. A government setting all prices describes a command economy.
A monopoly is a market with only one seller. With four shops on the block, Marlow's has more competition than ever.
items.explain: Before, Marlow's Cafe was the only seller on the street. Now buyers can switch, so Marlow's has a reason to lower prices or improve service. That is the basic effect of competition. Raising prices to make up for lost customers is the tempting error: in a competitive market, higher prices would drive even more customers to the new shops.

items.skill: Banks, the FDIC, and the Federal Reserve
items.prompt: Gloria keeps $260,000 in one individual savings account at an FDIC-insured bank. She has no other bank accounts. Which statements are accurate? Select two answers.
options: If her bank failed, the FDIC would cover $250,000 of Gloria's deposit.
The bank earns money partly by lending out deposits at a higher interest rate than it pays Gloria.
Gloria could protect the rest of her money by opening an account at the Federal Reserve.
The FDIC was created in 1913 to set interest rates for the nation's banks.
All $260,000 is insured, because the limit applies to each account, not each depositor.
why: Individuals cannot open accounts at the Federal Reserve. It serves banks and the federal government.
This mixes up the two agencies. The Federal Reserve was created in 1913 and influences interest rates; the FDIC was created in 1933 to insure deposits.
The limit is $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Gloria has one individual account, so $10,000 is over the limit.
items.explain: The FDIC insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category, so $250,000 of Gloria's $260,000 is covered and $10,000 is not. Banks earn much of their profit by lending deposits at a higher rate than they pay savers. The Fed does not take accounts from individuals, and the 1913 date belongs to the Federal Reserve, not the FDIC.

items.prompt: Based on the table, what was Country M's inflation rate from Year 2 to Year 3? Give your answer as a percent.

mistakes.why: That is the inflation rate from Year 1 to Year 2 (10 ÷ 250). The question asks about Year 2 to Year 3: 260 to 273.
13 is the change in the index (273 − 260). Divide it by the starting value to get a percent: 13 ÷ 260.
You divided by the new value (13 ÷ 273). Percent change divides by the starting value, 260.

items.explain:
Change in the price index: 273 − 260 = 13
Divide by the starting value: 13 ÷ 260 = 0.05
Convert: 0.05 × 100 = 5%

items.prompt:
Complete the statements.

Unemployment is rising across the country. To create jobs, Congress passes a law to {{0}} federal spending on highway and bridge projects. This is an example of {{1}} policy. To encourage borrowing, the Federal Reserve also {{2}} its target interest rate, which is an example of {{3}} policy.

options: increase
reduce
freeze
why: Cutting spending takes money out of the economy, which would not help a weak job market. To boost the economy, Congress spends more.
Freezing spending would not add money to a weak economy. To create jobs, Congress increases spending.

options: fiscal
monetary
trade
why: Monetary policy is the Federal Reserve's job. Congress changing federal spending is fiscal policy.
Trade policy covers imports, exports, and tariffs, not spending on highways.

options: lowers
raises
doubles
why: Raising rates makes borrowing more expensive and slows the economy. To help a weak economy, the Fed lowers rates.
Doubling the rate would make borrowing much more expensive and slow the economy further.

options: monetary
fiscal
antitrust
why: Fiscal policy is taxes and spending by Congress and the President. The Fed and interest rates mean monetary policy.
Antitrust policy is about competition and monopolies, not interest rates.

items.explain: To fight rising unemployment, Congress can increase spending, which is fiscal policy, and the Federal Reserve can lower its target interest rate, which is monetary policy. Both are meant to encourage spending and hiring. The common mix-up is calling the Fed's action fiscal; ask who acted and with what tool.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data in the table?
options: Workers' purchasing power rose from Year 1 to Year 2 but fell from Year 2 to Year 3.
Workers' purchasing power fell in both periods, because prices rose in both periods.
Higher wages in Year 2 caused prices to rise faster from Year 2 to Year 3.
Wages rose faster than prices from Year 1 to Year 2 and from Year 2 to Year 3.
why: Rising prices alone do not mean purchasing power fell. From Year 1 to Year 2, wages rose 5% while prices rose only 4%, so purchasing power rose.
The table shows wages and prices side by side; it does not show that one caused the other. "Caused" goes beyond the data.
From Year 2 to Year 3, wages rose only 2% ($0.42 ÷ $21.00) while prices rose 5% (13 ÷ 260).
items.explain:
Year 1 to Year 2: prices 10 ÷ 250 = 4%; wages $1.00 ÷ $20.00 = 5%. Wages beat prices, so purchasing power rose.

Year 2 to Year 3: prices 13 ÷ 260 = 5%; wages $0.42 ÷ $21.00 = 2%. Prices beat wages, so purchasing power fell.

The choice saying purchasing power fell in both periods is the trap: prices rose both times, but what matters is whether wages rose faster or slower.

items.prompt: The Brookdale city council has $2 million left in its budget. It could repave Main Street, buy new computers for the public library, or hire four more firefighters. The council votes to repave Main Street. Council records show that the library computers were the council's second choice. What is the opportunity cost of repaving Main Street?
options: The new library computers
Hiring four more firefighters
The library computers and the firefighters together
Nothing, since the money comes from taxes
why: Hiring firefighters ranked third on the council's list. Only the next best choice, the library computers, counts.
You added two options together. The council could spend the $2 million only once, so only its next best choice counts.
Governments face scarcity too. Tax money spent on one project cannot be spent on another, so the choice still has an opportunity cost.
items.explain: The opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up. The records show the library computers ranked second on the council's list. The "nothing" choice is tempting, but public money is scarce too: spending it on the road means giving up the computers.

items.prompt: If lawn-care visits cost $40 each, how many more visits per week would businesses offer than homeowners want?

mistakes.why: That is the gap at $45 (680 − 320). Use the $40 row: 580 − 400.
You added the two quantities (580 + 400). The size of a surplus is the difference between them.

items.explain:
At $40:
Quantity supplied = 580
Quantity demanded = 400
Supplied is bigger, so there is a surplus: 580 − 400 = 180 visits per week.

items.prompt: The price of home printers falls sharply, and many more people buy printers. What will most likely happen in the market for printer ink cartridges?
options: Demand for ink increases, and the price of ink tends to rise.
Demand for ink decreases, and the price of ink tends to fall.
Supply of ink increases, and the price of ink tends to fall.
Nothing changes, since only the price of printers changed.
why: That is how substitutes behave. Printers and ink are complements (used together), so more printers means more ink is wanted.
The event changes what buyers want, not what ink makers can produce. Ask first: buyers or sellers?
The price of a complement shifts demand. More people owning printers means more people need ink.
items.explain: Printers and ink are complements: goods used together. When printers get cheaper and more people buy them, more people need ink, so demand for ink increases and its price tends to rise. A decrease would fit substitutes, goods used instead of each other.

items.prompt: Which situation is most likely to be challenged under federal antitrust law, such as the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890?
options: The only two cement companies in a region secretly agree to raise prices together.
A software company becomes the most popular because its product is easier to use.
A new airline starts flying a route and charges half what the old airline charged.
A hardware store raises its prices after its own supplier's costs go up.
why: Becoming the most popular seller by offering a better product is not illegal. Antitrust law targets agreements and unfair tactics.
A new rival charging less is competition, which antitrust law is meant to protect.
One store raising prices because its costs rose is a normal business decision, not an agreement with competitors.
items.explain: The Sherman Antitrust Act makes it illegal for competitors to agree to fix prices or to use unfair tactics to build or keep a monopoly. The cement companies' secret agreement to raise prices together is exactly that. Being the most popular seller is the tempting wrong answer, but winning customers with a better product is not illegal.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly match a use of money with its function? Select two answers.
options: Comparing a $300 TV with a $450 TV uses money as a unit of account.
Saving $40 a week in a jar for a car repair next spring uses money as a store of value.
Paying a plumber $120 to fix a leak uses money as a unit of account.
Trading ten hours of tutoring for a car repair uses money as a medium of exchange.
Keeping extra cash at home during high inflation makes money a better store of value.
why: Money is changing hands for a service here, so it is a medium of exchange. A unit of account only measures or compares value.
No money changes hands in this trade. Trading services directly is barter, which money was invented to replace.
Inflation makes money a weaker store of value, because saved dollars buy less as prices rise.

vocab.def: The basic problem that people's wants are unlimited but the resources to satisfy them are limited.

vocab.def: The value of the next best alternative given up when making a choice.
vocab.example: If you skip a $60 shift to attend a class, the opportunity cost of the class is the $60.

vocab.def: The resources used to produce goods and services: land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship.
vocab.example: A bakery uses grain and water (land), bakers (labor), ovens (capital), and an owner's willingness to take a risk (entrepreneurship).

vocab.def: The amount of a product buyers are willing and able to buy at each price.
vocab.example: When a store cuts the price of jeans, it sells more pairs.

vocab.def: The amount of a product sellers are willing and able to offer at each price.

notes:
Week 7 Study Sheet: Economics

Scarcity: unlimited wants, limited resources, so every choice is a trade-off. Opportunity cost: the next best alternative given up (not the total of all options; "free" still has a cost). Factors of production: land (natural resources), labor (work), capital (tools, machines, buildings), entrepreneurship (risk-taking).

Supply and Demand

  • Law of demand: price up → quantity demanded down
  • Law of supply: price up → quantity supplied up
  • Equilibrium: demanded = supplied (lines cross)
  • Shortage: demanded > supplied (price too low)
  • Surplus: supplied > demanded (price too high)
  • Size: larger quantity − smaller quantity
  • Price ceiling (legal max, e.g., rent control) below equilibrium → shortage
  • Price floor (legal min, e.g., minimum wage) above equilibrium → surplus

What Shifts the Curves

  • Demand (buyers): income, tastes, price of substitutes (used instead) and complements (used together), expectations
  • Supply (sellers): input costs, technology, weather, taxes on producers, number of sellers
  • Demand up or supply down → price up
  • Demand down or supply up → price down
  • Routine: buyers or sellers? up or down? price?

Economic Systems and Competition

  • Market: buyers and sellers decide (Adam Smith, "invisible hand," 1776)
  • Command: government decides and sets prices
  • Mixed: mostly markets plus government rules and services (United States)
  • Competition → lower prices, better quality. Oligopoly: a few sellers. Monopoly: one seller
  • Sherman Antitrust Act (1890): bans price fixing and unfair monopoly tactics; being the only seller is not illegal by itself

Money and Banking

  • Money: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value (replaces barter)
  • Banks lend out much of their deposits and charge borrowers more interest than they pay savers
  • FDIC (1933): insures up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category
  • Federal Reserve (1913): central bank for banks and the government; monetary policy; goals of maximum employment and stable prices (about 2% inflation)
Fiscal policyMonetary policy
WhoCongress and the PresidentFederal Reserve
ToolsTaxes, spendingInterest rates, money supply
Boost a weak economyCut taxes / spend moreLower rates
Fight inflationRaise taxes / spend lessRaise rates

Measuring the Economy

  • GDP: value of all final goods and services produced in a country; real GDP is adjusted for inflation
  • Recession: real GDP falls and unemployment rises (rule of thumb: two quarters of falling GDP)
  • Inflation: general rise in prices (CPI); if pay rises more slowly than prices, purchasing power falls
  • Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. Always divide by the starting value.

GED tip: Read the title, labels, and units first. For events, ask "buyers or sellers?" For policy, ask "who acted, with what tool?" Answer from the data, and treat policy debates as "what does each side say?" not "which side is right?"
